protocol.goal_statement: Build from ~4,000 to a consistent 10,000 steps a day, anchored to a 20-30 minute lunch walk plus an after-work walk.
protocol.short_title: Walk 10,000 steps a day in 10 weeks

phases.title: Set the two slots
phases.focus: Get the lunch walk and the after-work walk happening on workdays, and let the daily number climb gently from where you already are.

steps.title: Lunch walk
steps.details: On each workday, get out for a 20-minute walk at lunch. Shoes and a jacket live under your desk so there's nothing to go find. If the day is slammed, 15 minutes still counts — the walk happens, it just gets shorter.

how_to.gist: 20 minutes out the door at lunch, every workday.
how_to.why: This is the walk that carries the whole goal. It's the one slot in a desk day where the time is already yours, and it's the difference between a 4,000-step day and a 7,000-step one.

sections.heading: The week
items: Monday to Friday: 20 minutes at lunch
Weekend: no lunch walk — the weekend walk covers it

sections.heading: Before you go
sections.body: Keep walking shoes and a light jacket under your desk or in a drawer. The walk should start within two minutes of you deciding to take it — no trip home, no changing clothes, no hunting for anything.

sections.heading: If work runs hot
sections.body: Shrink it, don't skip it. A 15-minute loop around the block at 1pm beats a 30-minute walk you keep pushing to tomorrow. Once you've skipped two lunch walks in a week, that's the signal to book it in your calendar like a meeting.

how_to.counts_as_done: You left the building and walked for at least 15 minutes on a workday.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 20 minutes, five workdays. Week 3 onward it stays at 20 minutes — this one doesn't grow, it just has to keep happening.

steps.title: After-work walk
steps.details: A 15-minute walk once work is done, before you sit down for the evening. Same route every day is fine — the point is that it's short enough that being tired is not a reason to skip it.

how_to.gist: 15 minutes on your feet right after work ends.
how_to.why: The lunch walk gets you most of the way; this one closes the gap and gets you out of the chair after a day of sitting. Keeping it short is deliberate — a walk you'll actually do beats a longer one you'll talk yourself out of.

sections.heading: When
sections.body: The moment work ends — before dinner, before the couch, before you open anything else. Change out of work clothes first if that helps you feel done for the day, then go.

sections.heading: Where
sections.body: Pick one default route and stop deciding. A loop from your front door that takes about 15 minutes is perfect. If you want variety, vary it on the weekend, not on a Tuesday when you're tired.

sections.heading: Tired evenings
sections.body: Tired is the normal state at this hour, so it can't be the deciding factor. Go out for five minutes with permission to turn around — most nights you'll keep going, and the nights you don't, you still logged the walk.

how_to.counts_as_done: You walked at least 10 minutes after finishing work.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 15 minutes, five workdays. It grows to 20 minutes in phase 2.

steps.title: Weekend walk
steps.details: One 30-minute walk on each weekend day. No desk, no lunch break — this is the day you have time, so use it to bank a bigger number and keep the streak alive.

how_to.gist: One 30-minute walk on Saturday and one on Sunday.
how_to.why: Weekends are where the weekly average gets rescued. Two solid walks here mean a rough Wednesday doesn't sink the week.

sections.heading: The week
items: Any time of day — morning, afternoon, or after dinner

sections.heading: Make it worth it
sections.body: Go somewhere you'd actually want to be — a park, a waterfront, a neighbourhood you like. If someone in your life will come along, bring them; a walk with company stops being a chore.

how_to.counts_as_done: 30 minutes of walking on that weekend day.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 30 minutes each weekend day. Grows to 40 minutes in phase 2 and 50 in phase 3.

steps.title: Daily step target
steps.details: Hit at least 5,000 steps a day in week 1, then add about 600 steps each week: 5,600 in week 2, 6,200 in week 3. Your phone or watch already counts this — just glance at it before bed.

how_to.gist: 5,000 steps a day this week, then about 600 more each week.
how_to.why: You're at roughly 4,000 now. Jumping straight to 10,000 is a wall; adding 600 a week is invisible. By week 10 the two walks plus your normal day get you there without any single day feeling like a leap.

sections.heading: How to check
sections.body: Whatever already counts your steps — phone in your pocket, watch on your wrist — is enough. Glance at it once in the evening so you know whether a short walk after dinner is needed to close the gap.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: The number is a weekly ladder, not a daily exam. If a day lands short, the next day's walks usually cover it. What matters is that the trend line climbs.

how_to.counts_as_done: Your step count for the day reads at or above this week's number.

steps.week_progression: Rises about 600 steps a week: 5,000 → 5,600 → 6,200 across phase 1.

steps.title: Set out tomorrow's walking kit
steps.details: Each evening before a workday, put your walking shoes and a jacket by the door or under your desk bag so the lunch walk starts without a single decision. Takes 30 seconds and removes the most common reason a walk doesn't happen.

how_to.gist: Shoes and jacket ready the night before, so the walk starts with zero setup.
how_to.why: The lunch walk dies in the two minutes you spend looking for shoes. Setting them out the night before means the walk is already half-started when lunch arrives.

sections.heading: What to set out
items: Walking shoes by the door or in your work bag
Anything else you'd otherwise go back inside for

sections.heading: When
sections.body: As part of whatever you already do before bed — after you set your alarm, after you brush your teeth, whenever it fits. It's a 30-second job, so it can ride along with something you already do.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: A desk day has no spare minutes. Anything that adds a step between you and the door is a reason to skip, and this removes all of them.

how_to.counts_as_done: Shoes and jacket were ready before you went to bed.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: five nights a week. From week 4 it's optional — by then the walk has its own momentum.

phases.title: Longer walks, higher floor
phases.focus: Both walks get longer and the daily number moves past 7,000. The lunch walk is now a fixed part of the workday.

steps.title: Lunch walk
steps.details: 25 minutes at lunch on each workday. Same slot, same shoes, five more minutes than last phase. On a genuinely impossible day, 15 minutes still counts.

how_to.gist: 25 minutes out at lunch, every workday.
how_to.why: Five extra minutes a day is about 500 extra steps across the week, and it's the cheapest place to find them — the time is already blocked out.

sections.heading: The change
sections.body: You've been doing 20 minutes for three weeks. Add five. If you want, extend the same route rather than inventing a new one — one extra block, one extra lap.

sections.heading: The floor
sections.body: 15 minutes is still the floor on a bad day. The walk never becomes zero.

how_to.counts_as_done: At least 15 minutes of walking at lunch on a workday.

steps.week_progression: 25 minutes through phase 2.

steps.title: After-work walk
steps.details: 20 minutes after work, up from 15. Same rule as before: it happens before you sit down for the evening, and 10 minutes is the floor on a rough night.

how_to.gist: 20 minutes on your feet after work.
how_to.why: This is the walk that closes the gap between your lunch walk and the day's number. It's still short enough to survive a tired evening.

sections.heading: The change
sections.body: Five more minutes than phase 1. Extend the same loop or add a second short one after dinner — either works.

sections.heading: The floor
sections.body: 10 minutes. Out the door and back is a win on the nights you have nothing left.

how_to.counts_as_done: At least 10 minutes of walking after work.

steps.week_progression: 20 minutes through phase 2.

steps.title: Weekend walk
steps.details: 40 minutes of walking on each weekend day. This is the walk that lets you bank a big number without touching your workday.

how_to.gist: 40 minutes of walking on Saturday and Sunday.
how_to.why: Weekend walks are where the weekly average gets pulled up. They're also the easiest walking you'll do all week — no clock, no desk.

sections.heading: The change
sections.body: Ten more minutes than phase 1. If 40 minutes in one go feels long, split it: 20 in the morning, 20 after dinner. Two walks count the same as one.

sections.heading: Make it stick
sections.body: Pick a destination — a coffee shop, a market, a park — so the walk has somewhere to go.

how_to.counts_as_done: 40 minutes of walking on that weekend day, in one go or split.

steps.week_progression: 40 minutes each weekend day through phase 2.

steps.title: Daily step target
steps.details: The ladder keeps climbing: 6,800 in week 4, 7,400 in week 5, 8,000 in week 6, 8,600 in week 7. Same 600-step weekly increase as before.

how_to.gist: 6,800 steps a day in week 4, climbing to 8,600 by week 7.
how_to.why: You're past the halfway point of the ladder. The longer walks in this phase are what make the bigger numbers possible without adding new habits.

sections.heading: If a week slips
sections.body: Repeat the same number for another week instead of moving up. The ladder only climbs when the last rung held — there's no prize for arriving early and no penalty for taking an extra week.

how_to.counts_as_done: Your step count for the day reads at or above this week's number.

steps.title: Add steps to the desk day
steps.details: On each workday, find one stretch of the day where you'd normally sit and stand instead: take the stairs, walk to a colleague instead of messaging, take calls on your feet, or park further away. One deliberate swap, not a whole new routine.

how_to.gist: One sitting stretch turned into standing or walking, each workday.
how_to.why: A desk job quietly eats 6,000 steps a day. You don't need to overhaul your workday — one swap a day is a few hundred steps, and it's the difference between hitting the number and chasing it at 9pm.

sections.heading: Pick one
items: Walk to someone's desk instead of messaging them
Take phone calls standing or pacing
Park at the far end of the lot
Refill your water bottle across the building

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: One swap a day is the target. Don't try to do all five — pick the one that fits your day and repeat it until it's automatic.

how_to.counts_as_done: You made one deliberate stand-or-walk swap during the workday.

steps.week_progression: One swap a day, five workdays, through phase 2.

phases.title: Ten thousand, held
phases.focus: The target reaches 10,000 and the job becomes holding it — including on the weeks life gets in the way.

steps.title: Lunch walk
steps.details: 30 minutes at lunch on each workday — the top of the range you named at the start. This is now the load-bearing walk of your day, so it gets protected like a meeting.

how_to.gist: 30 minutes out at lunch, every workday.
how_to.why: This is the walk you said you could do, at the length you said you could do it. It's carrying most of the 10,000, so it's the last thing to give up on a busy day.

sections.heading: Protect it
sections.body: Put it in your calendar as a recurring 30-minute block at the same time each day. When someone wants that slot, the walk wins or the walk moves — it doesn't disappear.

sections.heading: The floor
sections.body: 15 minutes. Even in your worst week, the lunch walk happens.

how_to.counts_as_done: At least 15 minutes of walking at lunch on a workday.

steps.week_progression: 30 minutes through phase 3.

steps.title: After-work walk
steps.details: 25 minutes after work. Together with the lunch walk, this is what puts 10,000 within reach on an ordinary day.

how_to.gist: 25 minutes on your feet after work.
how_to.why: Lunch walk plus this one plus your normal day is roughly 10,000 steps. Neither walk has to be heroic — they just both have to happen.

sections.heading: The change
sections.body: Five more minutes than phase 2. By now this walk should feel like part of the evening rather than something you decide to do.

sections.heading: The floor
sections.body: 10 minutes. Short walk beats no walk.

how_to.counts_as_done: At least 10 minutes of walking after work.

steps.week_progression: 25 minutes through phase 3.

steps.title: Weekend walk
steps.details: 50 minutes of walking on each weekend day. Long enough to be a proper outing, and it gives you slack for a short workday earlier in the week.

how_to.gist: 50 minutes of walking on Saturday and Sunday.
how_to.why: Weekend walks are your buffer. A big Saturday and Sunday means one rough Tuesday doesn't break the week.

sections.heading: The change
sections.body: Ten more minutes than phase 2. Split it if you like — 25 in the morning, 25 later.

sections.heading: Keep it enjoyable
sections.body: At this length, go somewhere worth going. A walk you look forward to is a walk that keeps happening after week 10.

how_to.counts_as_done: 50 minutes of walking on that weekend day, in one go or split.

steps.week_progression: 50 minutes each weekend day through phase 3.

steps.title: Daily step target
steps.details: 9,200 in week 8, 9,600 in week 9, and 10,000 in week 10 — the number you set out to reach. From week 10 on, 10,000 is the standing target.

how_to.gist: 9,200 in week 8, 9,600 in week 9, 10,000 in week 10.
how_to.why: This is the last stretch of the ladder. Ten weeks ago this number was a wall; now it's the walks you already do plus a normal day.

sections.heading: Holding 10,000
sections.body: Once you're at 10,000, the goal changes from climbing to holding. Aim for it most days rather than every single day — a week that averages 10,000 is a week you hit the goal, and chasing a perfect streak is how people quit at week 12.

sections.heading: If a week slips
sections.body: Drop back one rung and repeat it. You've already proven the walks work; a bad week is a scheduling problem, not a capability one.

how_to.counts_as_done: Your step count for the day reads at or above this week's number.

steps.title: Plan the week's walks
steps.details: Once a week, look at the week ahead and mark the days where the lunch walk or the after-work walk is genuinely at risk — a packed day, a late meeting, travel. Decide now which one moves and where it moves to, so a busy day bends the plan instead of breaking it.

how_to.gist: Once a week, spot the days the walks are at risk and decide now what moves.
how_to.why: At 10,000 steps a day there's no slack for a surprise. Five minutes on Sunday means a late meeting on Wednesday doesn't cost you the week.

sections.heading: What to look for
items: Days with back-to-back meetings over lunch
Evenings with something on after work
Travel or days away from your usual building
Anything that would normally make you skip

sections.heading: What to decide
sections.body: For each at-risk day, pick the fix in advance: walk at 11:30 instead of 1, do the after-work walk in the morning, or add 15 minutes to the weekend walk to cover it. Deciding on the day is how walks get skipped.

sections.heading: When
sections.body: Sunday evening or Monday morning, whichever you'll actually do. Five minutes, once a week.

how_to.counts_as_done: You looked at the week ahead and named which walks are at risk and what moves.

steps.week_progression: Once a week through phase 3.

milestones.title: Three weeks of walking at lunch
milestones.criteria: The lunch walk happened on at least 12 of the 15 workdays so far, and your daily average has climbed from about 4,000 to 6,200 steps.

milestones.title: Past 7,000 a day
milestones.criteria: Your weekly average is at or above 7,000 steps a day, and both the lunch walk and the after-work walk are happening without you having to talk yourself into them.

milestones.title: The walks are just what you do
milestones.criteria: Four weeks in a row where the lunch walk happened on every workday, and the after-work walk on at least four of five. The daily number is holding above 8,000.

milestones.title: 10,000 steps a day
milestones.criteria: Your weekly average is at or above 10,000 steps a day, built on the two walks you named at the start — a 30-minute lunch walk and a 25-minute walk after work.

protocol.coach_notes: You already did the hard part before we started: you named when the walking happens. Most people never get that far, and it's why their step goals die in week two. The number is going to feel almost insultingly small in week one — 5,000 steps when you're aiming for 10,000. That's on purpose. You're not building a step count, you're building two walks that will still be there in March. One missed day is noise; it's the day after a miss that decides whether this sticks, so if you skip a lunch walk, the next one is the one that matters. And if a week goes sideways, repeat the number instead of quitting the ladder — you've got ten weeks, and the rungs don't expire.

sessions.goal: I want to be able to run a 4k in six weeks. I basically neve

protocol.goal_statement: Run a continuous 4k — no walking breaks — in 10 weeks, starting from brisk walking with three morning runs a week.

phases.title: Getting the mornings to happen
phases.focus: Three mornings, same slot, same park. Week one is short on purpose — the win is showing up, not sweating.

steps.title: Morning walk-run session
steps.details: Out the door in the morning, trainers on, at the park. Warm up with 5 minutes of brisk walking, then alternate 1 minute of easy jogging with 2 minutes of walking for 15 minutes, then walk 5 minutes to finish. The jog is slow enough that you could talk in short sentences.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3 all use the same 1 min jog / 2 min walk shape. The only thing that changes is how many rounds you fit in — aim to add one round by week 3 if the last one felt easy.

how_to.gist: 25 min: 5 min brisk walk, then 1 min jog / 2 min walk, then 5 min walk home.
how_to.why: This is the whole plan in miniature. Short jogging bursts with walking in between let your legs and breathing adapt without the session ever turning into something you dread at 6am.

sections.heading: The shape
items: 5 min brisk walk to warm up

sections.heading: The pace
sections.body: The jog should be slow enough that you could say a short sentence out loud. If you're gasping, you're going too fast — slow down rather than cut the jog short. Walking briskly between bursts is part of the session, not a failure of it.

sections.heading: If it's rough
sections.body: If a jogging minute feels like too much, jog 30 seconds and walk 2 and a half. Same session, smaller dose. Finishing three mornings in a row matters far more than hitting an exact number of rounds.

how_to.counts_as_done: You got out and did the walk-jog-walk session, start to finish. Three of these in the week.

steps.title: Lay out everything the night before
steps.details: The night before each run morning, put your trainers, socks and a filled water bottle by the front door and set your alarm. Clothes laid out on the chair. Nothing to find, nothing to decide when you wake up.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: same routine every run eve. By week 3 it should take under a minute.

how_to.gist: Night before each run: trainers, socks, water by the door, alarm set.
how_to.why: The mornings you skip are almost never the ones where you decided not to run — they're the ones where you couldn't find a sock. Removing every small decision from the morning is what makes three mornings a week actually happen.

sections.heading: Before bed
items: Trainers and socks by the front door
Water bottle filled and next to them
Alarm set for the same time as always

sections.heading: Why the same time
sections.body: Same alarm, same slot, same park. The fewer things that vary between run mornings, the less there is to negotiate with yourself about at 6am.

how_to.counts_as_done: Everything was by the door and the alarm was set, the night before a run morning.

steps.title: Walk 30 minutes on the off days
steps.details: On two of your non-run days, take a 30-minute brisk walk. Same park or anywhere flat. This is not training for the run — it's keeping your legs used to moving on the days between, and it's the easiest thing in the plan to keep.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: two 30-minute walks. Keep them easy and conversational throughout.

how_to.gist: Two 30-minute brisk walks on days you're not running.
how_to.why: Three runs a week leaves four days where your legs do nothing. A couple of easy walks keeps the habit of moving daily and makes the run mornings feel less like a shock to the system.

sections.heading: When
sections.body: Tuesday and Saturday, or whichever two days sit furthest from your run mornings. Any time of day works — this one doesn't need to be before work.

sections.heading: How hard
sections.body: Brisk enough that you're breathing a bit harder than sitting, easy enough that you could hold a conversation the whole way. If you're puffing, slow down.

how_to.counts_as_done: Two 30-minute walks done this week, any two non-run days.

steps.title: Note how the last jogging minute felt
steps.details: Right after each morning session, while you're still catching your breath, decide one thing: could you have done one more jogging minute today, or was that the edge? That single answer is what tells you whether to add a round next week or hold where you are.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: same question after every session. It takes ten seconds and it's the only thing steering the plan.

how_to.gist: After each run, answer one question: one more minute left in the tank, or not?
how_to.why: You're building from zero, so the right next step depends entirely on how the last one felt. This one answer is what stops you from jumping ahead too fast or stalling out of caution.

sections.heading: The question
sections.body: Could you have jogged one more minute today? Yes or no. That's it — no times, no distances, no numbers to remember.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.body: Two or three 'yes' answers in a week means you're ready to add a round. Mostly 'no' means hold the same session another week. Either answer is fine; guessing is the only wrong move.

how_to.counts_as_done: You answered the question after each of the three sessions.

phases.title: Shrinking the walking
phases.focus: The walking breaks get shorter and the jogging stretches get longer. Same three mornings, same park.

steps.title: Morning walk-run session
steps.details: Same morning slot. Warm up with 5 minutes of brisk walking, then alternate 2 minutes of easy jogging with 1 minute of walking for 20 minutes, then walk 5 minutes to finish. The jog stays at the pace where you could talk in short sentences.
steps.week_progression: Week 4: 2 min jog / 1 min walk. Week 5: 3 min jog / 1 min walk. Week 6: 4 min jog / 1 min walk. Only move up when the previous week's last round felt manageable.

how_to.gist: 30 min: 5 min walk, then 2 min jog / 1 min walk for 20 min, 5 min walk.
how_to.why: The walking breaks are getting shorter and the jogging stretches longer — this is the part of the build where the running actually starts to feel like running instead of a series of sprints.

sections.heading: Moving up
sections.body: Each week the jogging stretch grows by a minute and the walking break stays at one. If a week's last round felt like the edge, repeat that week rather than pushing on — repeating a week costs you nothing, and pushing too early costs you a fortnight.

sections.heading: The pace
sections.body: Still conversational. As the jogging stretches get longer, the temptation is to speed up to get them over with. Don't. Slower jogging for longer is exactly the point.

how_to.counts_as_done: Three sessions done this week at the week's jog/walk shape.

steps.title: Lay out everything the night before
steps.details: Same routine as before: trainers, socks and water by the front door, clothes out, alarm set, the night before each run morning.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-6: unchanged. This is now just how run eves work.

steps.title: Walk 30 minutes on the off days
steps.details: Two 30-minute brisk walks on non-run days, same as before. Easy, conversational, any time of day.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-6: unchanged at two walks a week.

how_to.gist: Two 30-minute brisk walks on days you're not running.
how_to.why: Your run mornings are getting harder, so the days between matter more, not less. These walks keep your legs ticking over without adding any strain.

sections.heading: When
sections.body: Tuesday and Saturday, or whichever two days sit furthest from your run mornings.

sections.heading: How hard
sections.body: Conversational the whole way. If you're puffing, slow down.

how_to.counts_as_done: Two 30-minute walks done this week.

steps.title: Note how the last jogging stretch felt
steps.details: After each session, answer the same question: could you have jogged one more minute today? Two or three yeses in a week means move up a step next week; mostly noes means repeat the week.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-6: same question, and now it's deciding whether the jogging stretch grows each week.

how_to.gist: After each run: one more minute left in the tank, yes or no?
how_to.why: The jogging stretches are growing now, so this answer is doing more work than ever — it's the difference between a smooth build and a week you have to repeat.

sections.heading: The question
sections.body: Could you have jogged one more minute today? Yes or no, answered while you're still breathing hard.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.body: Mostly yeses: grow the jogging stretch next week. Mostly noes: repeat the same week. Repeating is a normal part of this, not a setback.

how_to.counts_as_done: You answered the question after each of the three sessions.

steps.title: Take an easy week if you need it
steps.details: If two sessions in a row felt like a grind, or your legs feel heavy and flat, drop back to the previous week's jog/walk shape for one week. Same three mornings, same length — just an easier shape. Then pick the build back up.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-6: use this at most once. It's a reset, not a routine.

how_to.gist: If two sessions in a row felt like a grind, repeat the previous week's easier shape.
how_to.why: Building from zero, the most common way people lose this goal is pushing through a flat patch and then quitting entirely. An easy week costs you seven days; a blown-out week costs you the plan.

sections.heading: When to use it
items: Two sessions in a row felt like a slog
Legs feel heavy and flat on a run morning
You're dreading the session rather than just not fancying it

sections.heading: What it looks like
sections.body: Drop back to the previous week's jog/walk shape and keep the same three mornings. You're not skipping sessions — you're doing easier ones. Next week, pick the build back up where you left off.

how_to.counts_as_done: You either didn't need it, or you took the easier week and ran all three mornings anyway.

phases.title: Closing the gaps
phases.focus: The walking breaks get shorter still, then disappear. The last two weeks are about holding a steady pace for the whole distance.

steps.title: Morning run session
steps.details: Same morning slot. Warm up with 5 minutes of brisk walking, then jog continuously for the session's target, then walk 5 minutes to cool down. The jog stays at the pace where you could talk in short sentences.
steps.week_progression: Week 7: 6 min jog / 1 min walk, repeated. Week 8: 10 min jog / 1 min walk, repeated. Week 9: jog 2.5k without stopping, then walk. Week 10: jog the full 4k without stopping.

how_to.gist: 35 min: 5 min walk, then the week's continuous jog, then 5 min walk.
how_to.why: This is where the walking breaks come out for good. The distance you've been covering in pieces becomes one continuous run — the thing you actually set out to do.

sections.heading: The build
items: Week 7: 6 min jog, 1 min walk, repeat
Week 8: 10 min jog, 1 min walk, repeat
Week 10: jog the full 4k without stopping

sections.heading: The pace
sections.body: Slower than you think. The whole point of the last two weeks is covering the distance without stopping, not covering it fast. If you finish the 4k feeling like you could have gone a bit further, you ran it right.

sections.heading: If a week doesn't land
sections.body: If week 9's continuous 2.5k doesn't happen, repeat week 8 and try again the following week. The 4k is the last step of a ladder, not a cliff — there's no shame in taking the rung twice.

how_to.counts_as_done: Three sessions done this week at the week's target, start to finish.

steps.title: Lay out everything the night before
steps.details: Same routine, and it matters most now: trainers, socks and water by the front door, clothes out, alarm set, the night before each run morning.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 7-10: unchanged. The sessions are the longest they've been — protect the mornings.

steps.title: Walk 30 minutes on the off days
steps.details: Two 30-minute brisk walks on non-run days. Easy and conversational — these are recovery, not training.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 7-10: unchanged at two walks a week.

how_to.gist: Two 30-minute brisk walks on days you're not running.
how_to.why: With the longest runs of the plan in these weeks, the easy days between them are what let your legs turn up fresh on Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

sections.heading: When

sections.heading: How hard

steps.details: After each session, answer the same question: could you have jogged one more minute today? In these weeks a 'yes' on the last session of the week is your green light to move to the next step of the build.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 7-10: same question, now steering the final climb to a continuous 4k.

how_to.gist: After each run: one more minute left in the tank, yes or no?
how_to.why: The steps are big now — 6 minutes to 10 minutes to a continuous 2.5k. This answer is what tells you whether to take the next one or repeat the one you're on.

sections.heading: The question
sections.body: Could you have jogged one more minute today? Yes or no, answered before you've cooled down.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.body: A yes on the last session of the week means take the next step up. A no means repeat the week. Both are fine — the only thing that isn't fine is guessing.

how_to.counts_as_done: You answered the question after each of the three sessions.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 7-10: use this at most once, and not in week 10.

how_to.gist: If two sessions in a row felt like a grind, repeat the previous week's easier target.
how_to.why: The last four weeks are the hardest part of the build, and the temptation to push through a flat patch is strongest here. An easy week keeps you in the plan; a forced week takes you out of it.

Legs heavy and flat on a run morning
