milestones.title: Three weeks of mornings, no misses
milestones.criteria: Nine morning sessions done in the same slot, and the walk-jog-walk shape is starting to feel routine rather than daunting.

milestones.title: Jogging stretches longer than the walks
milestones.criteria: You're jogging 4 minutes at a time with only a 1-minute walk between, three mornings a week.

milestones.title: 2.5k without stopping
milestones.criteria: You jogged 2.5 kilometres in one go, no walking breaks, on a normal morning before work.

milestones.title: A continuous 4k
milestones.criteria: You ran 4 kilometres without a single walking break — the goal, ten weeks after you started from brisk walking.

protocol.coach_notes: Ten weeks sounds longer than six, but it's the version where the last two weeks feel like running rather than surviving. Your three mornings are the whole engine here — protect that slot and the rest takes care of itself. One missed morning is noise; the morning after a miss is the one that decides whether this sticks, so never let two go by in a row.

sessions.goal: Learn to bake a proper layered birthday cake from scratch in

protocol.goal_statement: Bake a proper layered birthday cake from scratch — sponge, filling, frosting, stacked and finished — within a month, on one long weekend session plus one weeknight per week.
protocol.short_title: Bake a layered birthday cake in 4 weeks

phases.title: Learn the sponge
phases.focus: Get one plain sponge right, twice, and set the kitchen up so Saturday starts without hunting for anything.

steps.title: Bake a two-layer sponge
steps.details: One long Saturday session: weigh everything out first, make a plain vanilla sponge, split it between two tins, bake, cool fully on a rack. No frosting today — today is about the sponge and nothing else.

how_to.gist: Make one plain vanilla sponge, split across two tins, cooled on a rack.
how_to.why: Every layer cake sits on a sponge that rose properly. Get this one thing right before you add frosting, filling or stacking to the job.

sections.heading: Before you start
items: Oven on to the recipe's temperature, rack in the middle
Weigh every ingredient into little bowls before you mix anything
Line the bottom of both tins with baking paper, grease the sides
Butter and eggs out of the fridge 30 minutes early — they mix far easier by hand

sections.heading: The mix
sections.body: Use a recipe written for a hand whisk — an all-in-one sponge or an oil-based one, not a recipe that starts with 'cream the butter and sugar until pale'. Whisk the wet things together, sift the dry things in, fold gently until you can't see any dry flour. Stop there. Over-mixing is what makes a sponge tough.

sections.heading: The bake
sections.body: Divide the batter as evenly as you can between the two tins — a ladle each, back and forth, is more even than eyeballing. Bake until the middle springs back when you press it and a skewer comes out clean. Cool in the tins 10 minutes, then turn out onto a rack and leave them completely cold before you touch them.

sections.heading: If it goes wrong
sections.body: A sunken middle usually means the oven door was opened too early or the batter was over-mixed. A flat, dense sponge usually means old baking powder. Neither is a disaster — note what happened and bake it again next Saturday.

how_to.counts_as_done: Two cooled sponge layers on the rack, made from scratch by you.

steps.week_progression: Week 1 only: this is the first sponge you've ever made. Expect it to be imperfect; the goal is finishing it, not perfecting it.

steps.title: Set up the baking cupboard and tins
steps.details: Weeknight session: put everything you need for a bake in one place — tins, whisk, scales, paper, spatulas, cooling rack — and check you have the core ingredients in date (flour, sugar, butter, eggs, baking powder, vanilla). Write your shopping list for Saturday.

how_to.gist: Gather the kit and check the core ingredients, then write Saturday's shopping list.
how_to.why: Most failed weekend bakes die at 9am because one ingredient is missing or the baking powder is three years old. Ten minutes on Wednesday buys you a clean Saturday.

sections.heading: The cupboard check
items: Baking powder — in date, this one matters most

sections.heading: The list
sections.body: Write down anything missing, plus whatever Saturday's recipe needs that you don't have. Keep the list on the fridge so Saturday-you doesn't have to think.

how_to.counts_as_done: Kit in one place, ingredients checked, shopping list written.

steps.week_progression: Week 1 only: a one-time setup. After this, the cupboard stays set up and Wednesday becomes a different job.

steps.title: Bake the sponge a second time
steps.details: Same recipe as last Saturday, same two tins. This time weigh the batter into the tins so both layers are the same thickness, and write down your bake time and how the middle looked when you took it out.

how_to.gist: Repeat last week's sponge, weighing the batter evenly between the tins.
how_to.why: One sponge is luck; two is a skill. Repeating the exact same recipe is how your hands learn what the batter should look and feel like before it goes in the oven.

sections.heading: What changes
sections.body: Same recipe, same tins, same temperature. The only new thing is precision: put the empty tin on the scales, zero it, and ladle batter in until both tins weigh the same. Even layers are what make a stacked cake look deliberate rather than lopsided.

sections.heading: Write it down
sections.body: On a scrap of paper or the recipe itself: the time it went in, the time it came out, and one word for how it looked. Next week you'll want to know whether your oven runs hot.

sections.heading: The test
sections.body: Press the middle with a fingertip — it should spring back and feel dry, not tacky. If it leaves a dent, give it three more minutes and test again.

how_to.counts_as_done: Two even sponge layers, cooled, with your bake time written down.

steps.week_progression: Week 1 only: the second bake of the same recipe, this time with even layers.

steps.title: Read the whole recipe before you bake
steps.details: Weeknight session: read Saturday's recipe end to end, twice. Note the order of operations, what has to be cold, what has to be room temperature, and how long the whole thing takes. Then get out anything that needs to come to room temperature.

how_to.gist: Read Saturday's recipe twice and pull out anything that needs to warm up.
how_to.why: Cake recipes fail on timing, not on skill — butter that's still cold, a filling that needed an hour to set. Reading ahead is the cheapest mistake you'll ever avoid.

sections.heading: Read for these
items: What needs to be room temperature
How long the whole bake takes, start to finish
Anything that has to rest or chill

sections.heading: Then do this
sections.body: Put the butter and eggs on the counter if Saturday's recipe wants them soft. Check the fridge for cream or mascarpone if a filling needs it. Move anything frozen to the fridge to thaw overnight.

sections.heading: Plan the slot
sections.body: Decide now what time you're starting Saturday and roughly when you'll be done. A bake with no start time slides to 4pm and then doesn't happen.

how_to.counts_as_done: Recipe read twice, ingredients out, Saturday's start time decided.

steps.week_progression: Week 1 only: build the read-ahead habit now and it carries you through the frosting and assembly weeks.

phases.title: Learn the frosting
phases.focus: Frosting gets its own weekend, done by hand, on a cold bowl — plus a filling you can actually taste.

steps.title: Make a hand-whisked buttercream
steps.details: Saturday session: make a full batch of buttercream by hand — butter soft but not greasy, icing sugar sifted, a splash of milk, whisked until it holds a swirl. Chill a metal bowl and your whisk beforehand; it makes the job much shorter.

how_to.gist: Whisk a full batch of buttercream by hand until it holds a swirl.
how_to.why: Frosting is the part your kit makes hardest, so it gets a whole session to itself — learned fresh, not at the end of a long bake with a tired arm.

sections.heading: Set up for your arm
items: Butter out of the fridge at least an hour — soft, not melted
Sift the icing sugar, lumps will never whisk out
Chill a metal bowl and the whisk in the freezer for 10 minutes
A splash of milk on standby, not poured in yet

sections.heading: The whisking
sections.body: Beat the butter alone first until it's smooth and lighter in colour — this takes longer by hand than you expect, around 5 minutes. Then add the icing sugar in four or five goes, whisking each in fully before the next. Add milk a teaspoon at a time only if it's too stiff to move. Keep going until it holds a soft peak and doesn't slide off the whisk.

sections.heading: If it looks wrong
sections.body: Curdled or grainy almost always means the butter was too cold or the sugar went in too fast — keep whisking, or sit the bowl in warm water for 20 seconds and whisk again. If it's soupy, it's too warm: 15 minutes in the fridge, then whisk.

sections.heading: Store it
sections.body: Cover the surface with cling film so it doesn't crust, and keep it somewhere cool. It'll be fine for a day or two.

how_to.counts_as_done: A bowl of buttercream that holds a swirl, made by hand.

steps.week_progression: Week 2 only: first frosting attempt. It will take longer than the recipe says — that's the hand whisk, not you.

steps.title: Make a filling you can taste
steps.details: Same Saturday session, after the frosting: make one filling — jam, lemon curd, or a whipped cream and fruit mix. Taste it on a scrap of sponge and adjust the sugar or lemon until it's something you'd want a second spoon of.

how_to.gist: Make one filling and taste it on a scrap of sponge before you commit.
how_to.why: A layered cake is sponge, filling, frosting — the filling is the layer people actually remember. Making it on its own day means you're judging it on taste, not on how tired you are.

sections.heading: Pick one
items: Raspberry or strawberry jam, warmed and sieved smooth
Lemon curd, sharp enough to cut the buttercream
Whipped cream with soft fruit folded through

sections.heading: Taste it properly
sections.body: Spread a little on a piece of plain sponge and eat it. Too sweet? More lemon. Too sharp? A spoon of sugar. The filling has to taste good against the frosting, not on its own — so taste them together.

sections.heading: Keep it safe
sections.body: Anything with cream or curd goes straight in the fridge, covered. Jam can sit in a jar. Don't leave a cream filling on the counter overnight.

how_to.counts_as_done: One filling made and tasted on sponge, stored properly.

steps.week_progression: Week 2 only: the filling gets made and judged on its own, before it ever has to hold a cake up.

steps.title: Practise frosting on a spare sponge
steps.details: Weeknight session: frost the top of one plain sponge or a stack of biscuits — just to get the spatula movement into your hands. Thin crumb coat, then a second pass. Twenty minutes, no pressure, nothing riding on it.

how_to.gist: Frost a spare sponge or some biscuits just to practise the spatula movement.
how_to.why: Spreading frosting is a hand skill, and the first time you do it shouldn't be on the cake that matters. Twenty low-stakes minutes here saves the real cake.

sections.heading: What to practise
items: A thin first pass to lock the crumbs in
A second, thicker pass over the top
Turning the plate as you spread, not your wrist
Wiping the spatula clean between strokes

sections.heading: The point
sections.body: You're not making anything pretty. You're learning how much pressure to use and how the frosting behaves when it's cool versus warm. Warm frosting drags; cool frosting spreads.

sections.heading: Then stop
sections.body: Twenty minutes and you're done. This is a warm-up, not a bake.

how_to.counts_as_done: Twenty minutes of spreading frosting on something that doesn't matter.

steps.week_progression: Week 2 only: a low-stakes practice run before frosting touches a real cake.

steps.title: Read Saturday's frosting recipe twice
steps.details: Weeknight session: read the frosting and filling recipes end to end, note what has to be cold and what has to be soft, and put the butter out to soften overnight.

how_to.gist: Read the frosting and filling recipes, then put the butter out to soften.
how_to.why: Buttercream lives or dies on butter temperature, and butter takes hours to soften. Reading ahead is the whole trick.

sections.heading: Note these
items: How soft the butter needs to be
Whether the bowl should be cold
How much icing sugar, in total
Whether it needs chilling before use

sections.heading: Do these tonight
items: Butter out of the fridge onto the counter
Metal bowl and whisk into the freezer
Icing sugar checked — enough for a full batch

how_to.counts_as_done: Recipes read, butter softening on the counter.

steps.week_progression: Week 2 only: the same read-ahead habit, now aimed at the trickiest thing in the plan.

phases.title: Stack and finish
phases.focus: Build a real two-layer cake — levelled, filled, stacked, crumb-coated, then finished — and learn to fix it when it leans.

steps.title: Bake and level two sponge layers
steps.details: Saturday session: bake the two layers, cool them completely, then level the domed tops flat with a serrated knife so both layers sit square. Keep the offcuts — they're your taste test.

how_to.gist: Bake two layers, cool fully, then slice the domed tops flat.
how_to.why: A cake that leans almost always started with a domed layer. Levelling takes two minutes and is the difference between stacked and slumped.

sections.heading: Cool properly
sections.body: Completely cold, not warm. Frosting on a warm sponge slides off and the layers shift. If you're short on time, cool them on a rack in front of an open window.

sections.heading: Levelling
sections.body: Put the layer on a board, rest your hand flat on top, and saw gently with a serrated knife at the height of the dome's base. Keep the knife level — you're slicing, not pressing. Do the same to the second layer.

sections.heading: Keep the offcuts
sections.body: Eat one now to check the sponge tastes good, and keep the rest for crumbling over the top later.

how_to.counts_as_done: Two flat, cold, level sponge layers.

steps.week_progression: Week 3 only: the first time levelling matters, because this is the first cake that gets stacked.

steps.title: Stack and crumb coat the cake
steps.details: Same Saturday session: put layer one on the plate, spread the filling to the edge, add layer two, then cover the whole thing in a thin crumb coat and chill it for 30 minutes until it's set and firm.

how_to.gist: Fill between the layers, then a thin crumb coat over the whole cake and chill it.
how_to.why: The crumb coat is the step that makes the finished cake look clean — it traps all the loose crumbs under a thin layer so the final coat goes on smooth.

sections.heading: Stacking
items: A smear of frosting on the plate first, to stop it sliding
Layer one down, flat side up
Filling spread to the edge, roughly even thickness
Layer two on top, flat side down
Press gently and check it's level from the side

sections.heading: The crumb coat
sections.body: Thin. You should still see sponge through it in places. Work from the top down and turn the plate as you go. Don't fuss over how it looks — it's a primer, not the finish.

sections.heading: Chill it
sections.body: Thirty minutes in the fridge until the frosting is firm to a light touch. This is what stops the final coat dragging the crumb coat around.

how_to.counts_as_done: A stacked, filled, crumb-coated cake, chilled and firm.

steps.week_progression: Week 3 only: first stacked cake. If it leans, straighten it now while the frosting is still soft.

steps.title: Finish the cake
steps.details: Same Saturday session, after the chill: a second, thicker coat of frosting over the whole cake, smoothed with a warm spatula, then whatever finish you want — swirls, a rim of crumbs, fruit on top.

how_to.gist: Second, thicker coat of frosting, smoothed with a warm spatula, then a finish.
how_to.why: This is the coat people see. Because the crumb coat is underneath, this one goes on smooth and you can actually enjoy doing it.

sections.heading: The second coat
sections.body: More frosting than the crumb coat, spread from the top outwards and down the sides. Dip your spatula in hot water and dry it between strokes — warm metal smooths frosting like nothing else.

sections.heading: The finish
items: Swirl the top with the back of a spoon
Press crumbs around the bottom edge
Fresh fruit on top, added just before serving
Nothing at all — a clean smooth cake is a finish

sections.heading: If it leans or bulges
sections.body: Chill it for 20 minutes, then press the layers back into line with a flat hand and patch the frosting over the seam. Nobody will know.

how_to.counts_as_done: A fully frosted, finished cake on a plate.

steps.week_progression: Week 3 only: the first complete cake, start to finish.

steps.title: Plan the real cake's flavour and timing
steps.details: Weeknight session: decide the flavour of the birthday cake — sponge, filling, frosting — write the shopping list, and work out the timeline for next Saturday so the cake is finished the day before it's needed, not the morning of.

how_to.gist: Choose the birthday cake's flavours, write the list, and set next Saturday's timeline.
how_to.why: Next week is the real thing. Deciding flavours and timings on Wednesday means Saturday is only about baking, not about decisions.

sections.heading: Choose
items: Filling — jam, curd, cream and fruit
One finish you can actually pull off

sections.heading: The timeline
sections.body: Work backwards from when the cake is needed. Bake and cool Saturday morning, fill and crumb coat after lunch, final coat late afternoon, chill overnight. Frosting a cake the day before makes it easier to slice and takes all the panic out of the morning.

sections.heading: The list
sections.body: Everything for the full cake, in one shop, plus a spare block of butter and a spare bag of icing sugar. Running out mid-frost is the worst way to lose an afternoon.

how_to.counts_as_done: Flavours chosen, timeline written, shopping list made.

steps.week_progression: Week 3 only: the planning session that sets up the real bake.

phases.title: Bake the birthday cake
phases.focus: Do the whole thing clean, in one go, on the timeline you wrote — and have a rescue plan ready if a layer breaks.

steps.title: Bake the birthday cake
steps.details: The real bake, following your own timeline: sponge, cool, level, fill, stack, crumb coat, chill, finish. Same recipes you've already made twice. Work steadily and don't add anything new on the day.

how_to.gist: The full cake, start to finish, on the timeline you wrote — nothing new.
how_to.why: You've made every part of this already. Today is about doing them in order, calmly, without inventing anything on the spot.

sections.heading: The order
items: Weigh everything out before you mix

sections.heading: The rule for today
sections.body: Nothing new. Same sponge recipe, same frosting method, same filling you've already tasted. New recipes on the day of the real bake are how good cakes become average ones.

sections.heading: If a layer breaks
sections.body: Press the pieces back together on the plate — the filling and frosting will hold them. If it's beyond saving, use the broken layer as the bottom one and cover it with the good one. Nobody sees the bottom layer.

how_to.counts_as_done: A finished layered birthday cake, chilled and ready.

steps.week_progression: Week 4 only: the real bake, using recipes you've already made at least twice.

steps.title: Do the Wednesday read-ahead and shop
steps.details: Weeknight session: shop for the full cake from your list, read the recipes once more, and put the butter out to soften. Everything in the kitchen ready so Saturday starts at the mixing bowl.

how_to.gist: Shop from the list, re-read the recipes, butter out to soften.
how_to.why: The last thing you want on the day of the real bake is a trip to the shop. This session exists so Saturday has no gaps in it.

sections.heading: Shop
sections.body: From the list you wrote last week, plus spares: an extra block of butter, an extra bag of icing sugar, an extra punnet of fruit if you're using it.

sections.heading: Set up
items: Tins greased and lined, ready to go
Plate or board for the finished cake chosen
Spatula, knife, and a jug of hot water for smoothing

how_to.counts_as_done: Everything bought and laid out, butter softening.

steps.week_progression: Week 4 only: the last prep session — after this the plan is done.

steps.title: Write down what you'd change next time
steps.details: After the cake is eaten: five minutes writing what worked, what you'd do differently, and which recipe you'd keep. One page, kept with your recipes.

how_to.gist: Five minutes writing what worked and what you'd change next time.
how_to.why: You've just learned four skills in a month. Writing them down is what turns this from a one-off birthday cake into something you can do again on request.

sections.heading: Answer three things
items: Which recipe would you make again exactly as it was?
What took longer than you expected?
What would you change about the frosting or the filling?

sections.heading: Keep it
sections.body: One page, with your recipes. Next time someone asks for a cake, you start from your own notes instead of a stranger's recipe.

how_to.counts_as_done: One page of notes written and kept with your recipes.

steps.week_progression: Week 4 only: the last rep of the plan.

milestones.title: You baked a sponge from scratch
milestones.criteria: Two sponge layers made and cooled, twice over, with your bake time written down.

milestones.title: Buttercream by hand, and it held
milestones.criteria: A bowl of hand-whisked buttercream that holds a swirl, plus a filling you tasted and adjusted.

milestones.title: A stacked, frosted cake on a plate
milestones.criteria: Two levelled layers, filled, stacked, crumb-coated, chilled and finished.

milestones.title: The birthday cake, done
milestones.criteria: The full layered cake baked, stacked and finished on your own timeline, with notes written for next time.

protocol.coach_notes: Four weekends, four bakes, one skill each — that's the whole plan, and it's why a month is enough. The only thing that will actually trip you up is your arm: buttercream by hand takes longer than any recipe admits, so give it its own Saturday and don't judge yourself by the clock. If a Saturday gets away from you, don't try to double up the next day — just do the next bake on the list. One missed weekend is nothing; two in a row is how a plan like this quietly dies.

sessions.goal: Read 10 minutes before bed every night for the next month.

protocol.goal_statement: Read 10 minutes in bed every night for the next month — book on the nightstand, phone out of arm's reach.

phases.title: Swap the nightstand
phases.focus: Get the book where your hand already goes and the phone somewhere else. Ten minutes, every night, no exceptions for mood.

steps.title: Put the book where the phone sits
steps.details: One-time setup, done before your first night: the book goes flat on the nightstand in the exact spot the phone has been living, and the phone's charger moves to the far side of the room — dresser, desk, hallway outlet, anywhere you can't reach from the pillow. Do it now, not tonight when you're tired.

how_to.gist: Book on the nightstand, phone charger across the room — done today.
how_to.why: Last time the scroll won because the phone was the thing within reach and the book wasn't. This one swap does most of the work for the whole month, so it's worth doing before you're tired and negotiating with yourself.

sections.heading: The swap
items: Take the phone charger off the nightstand and plug it in across the room
Put the book flat in the spot the phone used to sit
Put the phone on the far charger before you get into bed tonight

sections.heading: Pick the book
sections.body: Something you actually want to read, not something you think you should. A novel you've been meaning to start beats a dense book you'll avoid. If the current book bores you, swap it now — a boring book is a phone in disguise.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: The nightstand spot belongs to the book from here on. If the phone ends up back on it, that's the whole plan undone, so treat the charger's new home as permanent.

how_to.counts_as_done: Book on the nightstand and phone charging across the room, tonight.

steps.title: Read 10 minutes in bed
steps.details: Once you're in bed, pick up the book and read for ten minutes. Phone stays on the far charger. Ten minutes is the floor, not a warm-up — if you're into it at ten, keep going; if you're wrecked, ten is a full rep.

how_to.gist: In bed, book in hand, ten minutes before you settle down.
how_to.why: Ten minutes is small enough to survive a bad night, which is the point — this is the rep that has to hold on the nights you're tired, and most nights you will be.

sections.heading: The slot
sections.body: You're in bed around 11 most nights. That's the slot — the reading happens right when you land, before you'd normally reach for anything else. No deciding whether tonight is a reading night; it's every night.

sections.heading: The ten minutes
sections.body: Book open, phone across the room. Read until ten minutes are up. If the page is pulling you in, keep reading — the ten is a floor. If you're half asleep, ten minutes still counts as done.

sections.heading: Wrecked nights
sections.body: Two minutes counts on a night you're genuinely done in. What doesn't count is zero — a two-minute night keeps the chain alive, and the chain is what makes this stick.

how_to.counts_as_done: Ten minutes with the book open in bed (two minutes on a wrecked night), phone not in reach.

steps.title: Phone on the far charger before you get in bed
steps.details: Plug the phone in across the room before you get into bed — not after, not once you've had a look at it. If it's in your hand when you climb in, it's already won the night.

how_to.gist: Phone on the far charger before you climb into bed.
how_to.why: The phone is the incumbent habit here, and distance is the only thing that reliably beats it. A phone across the room is a phone you mostly don't pick up.

sections.heading: Why before, not after
sections.body: If you get into bed with the phone, you'll use it — that's the pattern that beat you last time. Plugging it in first means the reach you'd normally make comes up empty and the book is what your hand finds.

sections.heading: If it slips
sections.body: If the phone ends up in bed with you, put it back on the charger and read your ten minutes anyway. The night isn't lost; the streak isn't either.

how_to.counts_as_done: Phone plugged in across the room before you got into bed.

steps.title: Lights out by 11:15
steps.details: You land in bed around 11, so reading ten minutes puts you at lights-out around 11:15. Keep that landing time steady — a consistent bedtime is what turns the reading slot into something you do without thinking about it.

how_to.gist: Book down, lights out around 11:15 — same landing time every night.
how_to.why: A steady bedtime makes the reading slot automatic instead of a nightly decision. When the same thing happens at the same time every night, you stop having to choose it.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: In bed around 11, ten minutes of reading, lights out around 11:15. That's the shape of the night — you're not adding time to your evening, you're filling the slot where the scrolling used to be.

sections.heading: Weekends too
sections.body: Same landing time on weekends. A late Saturday resets the whole thing and makes Monday a decision again, which is exactly what you're trying to get away from.

sections.heading: If you're not sleepy
sections.body: Lights out at 11:15 even if you're not drowsy. Lying there with the book closed is fine — the point is that the phone isn't the last thing you see.

how_to.counts_as_done: Lights out by 11:15.

phases.title: Make it the default
phases.focus: Same setup, longer stretch — the reading gets a little more room and the phone stays where it belongs.

steps.title: Read 15 minutes in bed
steps.details: The floor goes up to fifteen minutes. You've had two weeks of ten; fifteen is a small stretch, not a new habit. Two-minute nights still count if you're genuinely wrecked.

how_to.gist: Same night, same book — fifteen minutes instead of ten.
how_to.why: Ten minutes proved the swap works. Fifteen is where the reading starts to feel like the thing you do at night rather than a task you're fitting in.

sections.heading: The change
sections.body: Everything about the night stays the same — phone on the far charger, book in the nightstand spot, in bed around 11. The only difference is the clock: fifteen minutes instead of ten.

sections.heading: Still a floor
sections.body: If the book is good, read past fifteen. If you're wrecked, two minutes still counts. The number moved; the rule didn't.

how_to.counts_as_done: Fifteen minutes with the book open in bed (two minutes on a wrecked night).

steps.title: Phone on the far charger before you get in bed
steps.details: Same rule, held for another two weeks. This is the one that decides whether the habit survives past the month — the book is easy once the phone is out of reach.

how_to.gist: Phone on the far charger before you climb into bed — every night.
how_to.why: Two weeks in, the temptation is to let the phone back onto the nightstand because the reading is going fine. That's the exact move that killed this last time.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Phone on the far charger before you get into bed. No exceptions for "just checking one thing" — that's how the night starts and how the book stays closed.

sections.heading: If it slips
sections.body: Put it back and read anyway. One night of the phone winning doesn't undo two weeks; two nights in a row is where it starts to.

how_to.counts_as_done: Phone plugged in across the room before you got into bed.

steps.title: Lights out by 11:15
steps.details: Hold the same landing time through the last two weeks. Fifteen minutes of reading still puts you out around 11:15 — the bedtime doesn't move just because the reading got longer.

how_to.gist: Lights out by 11:15, same as the first two weeks.
how_to.why: The steady landing time is what makes the whole night run without decisions. Moving it now would hand the choice back to you every evening.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: In bed around 11, fifteen minutes of reading, lights out around 11:15. Same shape as before, slightly longer read.

sections.heading: Weekends too
sections.body: Same time Saturday and Sunday. The habit is the whole week or it isn't a habit.

how_to.counts_as_done: Lights out by 11:15.

steps.title: Finish the book you started
steps.details: One-time rep for the last two weeks: get to the end of the book you've been reading at night. Finishing something is the proof that the ten minutes added up to more than ten minutes.

how_to.gist: Read the last page of the book you started this month.
how_to.why: Four weeks of ten and fifteen minutes adds up to a finished book, and a finished book is the thing that makes you want to start the next one.

sections.heading: The rep
sections.body: Finish the book you've been reading in bed. If you finish early, start the next one — the nightstand spot doesn't go empty.

sections.heading: If it's a long one
sections.body: If the book is genuinely long, this rep is "pick the next book and put it on the nightstand." The point is that the slot stays filled.

how_to.counts_as_done: Reached the last page, or the next book is on the nightstand.

milestones.title: Seven nights, book in hand
milestones.criteria: Seven nights in a row with the book open in bed and the phone on the far charger. The setup is done and the first week is behind you.

milestones.title: Two weeks and the phone hasn't moved back
milestones.criteria: Fourteen nights of reading, and the nightstand still belongs to the book. This is the point where last time's attempt fell apart.

milestones.title: Fifteen minutes feels normal
milestones.criteria: A full week at fifteen minutes a night, with the phone across the room every one of those nights.

milestones.title: A month of nights, and a finished book
milestones.criteria: Twenty-eight nights of reading in bed and the book you started this month is done. The nightstand swap held for a full month.

protocol.coach_notes: The reading was never the hard part — the phone on the nightstand was. That's why the first thing this plan does is move furniture, not motivate you. One missed night is noise; the night after a miss is the one that decides whether this is a habit or another attempt. Keep the phone across the room and the book will take care of itself.

sessions.goal: Quit smoking over the next three months. I smoke about 10 a

protocol.goal_statement: Quit smoking for good over four months — a two-week taper down from 10 a day, a hard quit date after it, and a specific plan for the two danger zones (the after-meal cigarette and the evening drink), with nicotine replacement on board from day one.

phases.title: Taper and get ready
phases.focus: Two weeks walking 10 a day down to 3, with the after-meal and work-break cigarettes moved out of their usual spots and the evening drink hour rebuilt before quit day arrives.

steps.title: Smoke no more than your taper number
steps.details: Week 1: no more than 7 a day. Week 2: no more than 3 a day. Count them — the number is the whole point of these two weeks.
steps.week_progression: Week 1 cap 7 a day, week 2 cap 3 a day, then zero from quit day onward.

how_to.gist: Cap it at 7 a day this week, 3 next week, then none.
how_to.why: You've gone cold turkey twice and lost it at week two. Walking down instead of jumping off means quit day arrives with a much smaller habit to fight.

sections.heading: The numbers
items: Week 1: no more than 7 a day
Week 2: no more than 3 a day

sections.heading: How to count
sections.body: Keep the pack and a pen together. Every cigarette gets a tick on the back of the pack the moment you light it. If you're at your number by 6pm, the rest of the evening is done — that's the deal you made with yourself this morning.

sections.heading: If you go over
sections.body: Don't restart the week. Note the number, finish the day, and hold the cap tomorrow. Two over on a Tuesday doesn't undo the taper.

how_to.counts_as_done: The day's ticks are at or under the cap — 7 in week 1, 3 in week 2.

steps.title: Move the after-meal cigarette
steps.details: After every meal, get up and do something with your hands and mouth for ten minutes instead of sitting where you'd normally light up — brush your teeth, clear the plates, walk to the end of the street.

how_to.gist: Ten minutes of moving after every meal, away from where you smoke.
how_to.why: After meals is one of your two automatic moments. The cigarette isn't really the point there — the sitting-down-and-finishing is. Change what happens in those ten minutes and the cigarette loses its slot.

sections.heading: The ten minutes
items: Stand up the second you finish eating
Brush your teeth, or clear the plates, or step outside and walk
Stay out of your usual smoking spot
Come back when the ten minutes are up

sections.heading: Why teeth
sections.body: A clean mouth makes a cigarette taste bad for about twenty minutes. That's twenty minutes you don't have to argue with yourself.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: One after-meal cigarette doesn't mean the day is gone. Do the ten minutes at the next meal anyway — the routine is what you're building, not a perfect record.

how_to.counts_as_done: You did the ten minutes after each meal you ate at home or at work today.

steps.title: Take your work break without smoking
steps.details: On work days, take the same break at the same time but don't go to the smoking spot. Walk a different route, or stay in and make a drink, and be back when the break ends.

how_to.gist: Same break, same time, different place — not the smoking spot.
how_to.why: Stepping out at work is your other automatic moment. The break itself is fine; it's the standing-in-the-smoking-spot part that hands you a cigarette. Keep the break, change the address.

sections.heading: The swap
items: Take the break at the usual time
Walk a route that doesn't pass the smoking spot
Bring something to do — a drink, a phone call, a short walk
Come back when the break ends

sections.heading: If people ask
sections.body: You don't owe anyone a speech. "Cutting back" is a complete answer.

sections.heading: The hard version
sections.body: If the smoking spot is the only place to stand outside, go further — round the block, or the far entrance. Distance is the whole trick.

how_to.counts_as_done: You took your work break today without going to the smoking spot.

steps.title: Rebuild the evening drink hour
steps.details: Every evening, have your drink with something in your other hand and something to do — a specific non-alcoholic drink you actually like, and a snack or a task. Same chair, same time, no cigarette.

how_to.gist: Drink in hand plus a second drink and a snack — no cigarette.
how_to.why: You told me evenings with a drink are the hardest part of the day. That hour is where this quit has the most to lose, so it gets a script instead of a hope.

sections.heading: The setup
items: Pour a second glass of something you actually like — sparkling water, tea, squash
Put a snack on the table
Keep your hands busy — cards, cooking, a game, tidying

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: No smoking while you're drinking. If you're going to smoke, you stand up, leave the drink, and go outside — you don't get both at once. Most nights you won't bother getting up.

sections.heading: If the craving hits
sections.body: It peaks and passes in a few minutes. Sip the second drink, chew the snack, and let it run out. You don't have to do anything about it except wait.

how_to.counts_as_done: You had your evening drink with the second drink and a snack, and no cigarette alongside it.

steps.title: Pick your quit day and get the patches in the house
steps.details: Choose the exact date quit day starts — the day after your two-week taper ends — write it somewhere you'll see it daily, and buy nicotine patches before that date so they're waiting.

how_to.gist: Name the date, write it down, buy the patches before it arrives.
how_to.why: Both times you quit cold turkey you had nothing on board and no date you could see coming. A date on the fridge and patches already in the drawer change the shape of that morning.

sections.heading: The date
sections.body: It's the day after your taper ends — two weeks from today. Pick a day of the week you can control: not a big night out, not a work deadline.

sections.heading: Where it goes
items: Set a phone reminder for the night before

sections.heading: The patches
sections.body: Buy a starter pack before the date. Ask the pharmacist which strength suits someone smoking about 10 a day — that's their job, and it takes two minutes.

how_to.counts_as_done: The date is written down somewhere you'll see it, and the patches are in the house.

steps.title: Tell one person your quit date
steps.details: Tell one person — partner, friend, or a colleague who sees you at break — the date you're quitting, and ask them to check in with you the week after it.

how_to.gist: One person knows the date and will ask you about it.
how_to.why: Week two is where this has died twice, and it died quietly. Someone who knows the date turns a private wobble into a conversation.

sections.heading: Who
sections.body: Pick someone you'd actually tell the truth to — not the person most likely to be impressed.

sections.heading: What to say
sections.body: "I'm quitting on the 14th. Can you ask me how it's going the week after?" That's the whole ask.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: You've done two weeks twice. Having someone expecting to hear from you is the difference between a slip you hide and a slip you mention on day one.

how_to.counts_as_done: You told one person the date and asked them to check in.

phases.title: Quit day and the first month
phases.focus: Zero cigarettes from quit day, patches on from the first morning, and the after-meal and drink-hour routines running on autopilot through the week-two danger zone.

steps.title: No cigarettes at all
steps.details: From quit day onward, zero. Not one, not a drag off someone else's — none. If you smoke one, the day is over and tomorrow starts clean.
steps.week_progression: Zero every day from quit day through the end of the plan.

how_to.gist: Zero cigarettes today — not one, not a drag.
how_to.why: This is the goal itself. Everything in the taper and the routines was building toward this morning.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: No cigarettes. Not one. The first one is the only one that matters, because it's the one that turns into ten.

sections.heading: If you smoke one
sections.body: The day is done, not the quit. Bin the pack, put a patch on tomorrow morning, and carry on. One cigarette in a month is a blip; a week of them is a relapse.

sections.heading: The first three days
sections.body: Expect to feel scratchy, foggy, and short-tempered. That's the nicotine leaving, not you failing. It eases off after about three days.

how_to.counts_as_done: Zero cigarettes today.

steps.title: Put a patch on every morning
steps.details: First thing after you wake up, before coffee, patch on. Same spot routine each day — rotate the site so your skin doesn't get sore.

how_to.gist: Patch on first thing in the morning, before coffee.
how_to.why: You've never used patches or gum. Cold turkey twice got you two weeks. This is the support that wasn't there the other two times.

sections.heading: When
sections.body: The moment you're up — before the coffee, before the phone. The morning cigarette is the one your body reaches for first, so the patch goes on before that window opens.

sections.heading: Where
items: Clean, dry skin above the waist
Press it flat for ten seconds

sections.heading: Follow the pack
sections.body: Use the strength and the step-down schedule the pharmacist gave you. Don't cut it short because you feel fine — feeling fine is the patch working.

how_to.counts_as_done: A patch is on your skin today.

steps.title: Keep the after-meal ten minutes
steps.details: Same as the taper weeks: after every meal, ten minutes up and moving, teeth brushed, away from the smoking spot.

how_to.gist: Ten minutes up and moving after every meal, teeth brushed.
how_to.why: This is the routine you built in the taper weeks, and now it's doing the real work. After meals is where the habit reaches for you hardest.

sections.heading: The ten minutes
items: Up the second you finish eating
Back when the ten minutes are done

sections.heading: The danger meal
sections.body: Whichever meal you most associate with a cigarette — that's the one to be strictest about. Plan what you'll do before you sit down to eat.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: Do the ten minutes at the next meal regardless. The routine is the thing that carries you, not a clean record.

how_to.counts_as_done: You did the ten minutes after each meal today.

steps.title: Run the drink hour without a cigarette
steps.details: Evening drink with the second drink and a snack on the table, no cigarette alongside it. If you want to smoke, you leave the drink and go outside.

how_to.gist: Drink, second drink, snack — and no cigarette with any of it.
how_to.why: You named evenings with a drink as the hardest part of your day. This is the hour that decides whether the quit holds.

sections.heading: The setup
items: A second drink you actually like
Something to do with your hands

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: No smoking while you're drinking. Standing up and leaving the drink to go outside is allowed — but you don't get both at once.

sections.heading: The hard nights
sections.body: If the drink is what makes you want a cigarette, have one or two fewer for a few weeks. You can pick the habit back up later; the quit is the thing that's fragile right now.

how_to.counts_as_done: You had your evening drink with no cigarette alongside it.

steps.title: Write down every craving you ride out
steps.details: When a craving hits and you don't smoke, put a tick on a note in your pocket or phone. One tick a day is the minimum — most days there'll be more.

how_to.gist: One tick for every craving you get through without smoking.
how_to.why: Week two is where this died twice, and the reason is that cravings feel endless when you can't see them ending. Ticks make them countable — and countable things end.

sections.heading: What counts
sections.body: Any moment you wanted a cigarette and didn't have one. Ten seconds of wanting counts the same as ten minutes.

sections.heading: Where
sections.body: Back of your phone notes, or a scrap of paper in your pocket. Somewhere you'll see it again the same day.

sections.heading: What it's for
sections.body: On a bad evening, look at the ticks. Every one of them is a craving that already ended. That's the evidence that this one will too.

how_to.counts_as_done: At least one tick on the list today.

steps.title: Check in with your person
steps.details: Once a week, tell the person you told your quit date to how the week actually went — the good days and the bad ones.

how_to.gist: One honest weekly update to the person who knows your quit date.
how_to.why: Both relapses happened in private. A weekly report to one person makes a wobble something you say out loud instead of something you act on.

sections.heading: The update
items: The hardest moment of the week
Whether you slipped, and what set it off

sections.heading: Be straight
sections.body: The point isn't to look good, it's to catch a bad week early. A slip you mention on day one is a slip you can stop.

sections.heading: Week two especially
sections.body: That's the week it went wrong twice before. If you're going to lean on this person, lean hardest then.

how_to.counts_as_done: You gave your person an honest update this week.

phases.title: Steady and step the patches down
phases.focus: The quit is normal now — this phase is about stepping the patches down on schedule, keeping the routines through the days that used to be automatic, and handling the odd rough day without treating it as a crisis.

steps.title: No cigarettes at all
steps.details: Still zero. This is the stretch where it stops feeling like effort and starts feeling like who you are — keep the count at zero anyway.
steps.week_progression: Zero every day, same as phase 2 — the difference now is that it's routine rather than a fight.

steps.title: Step the patch down on schedule
steps.details: Follow the pharmacist's step-down plan — move to the lower strength when the pack says to, not when you feel brave. Keep wearing it daily until the course is done.

how_to.gist: Move to the lower patch strength when the schedule says, not before.
how_to.why: Coming off the patches too early is the quiet version of the cold turkey you've already tried twice. The step-down is what makes the landing soft.

sections.heading: The schedule
sections.body: Whatever the pharmacist wrote on the pack — usually a few weeks at the higher strength, then a few at the lower. Follow the dates, not your mood.

sections.heading: If it gets rough
sections.body: A rough few days after a step-down is normal and temporary. If it's genuinely unbearable, go back up a step for another week and try again — that's not failure, that's the plan working.

sections.heading: The end
sections.body: When the course finishes, you stop. By then the physical part is long done and what's left is routine — which you've already rebuilt.

how_to.counts_as_done: You're on the patch strength the schedule calls for today.

steps.title: Keep the after-meal ten minutes
steps.details: Still ten minutes up and moving after every meal. By now it should feel like the normal end of a meal.
steps.week_progression: Same routine, but it's no longer a fight — the goal is that skipping it would feel odd.

steps.title: Keep the drink hour script
steps.details: Evening drink with the second drink and a snack, no cigarette alongside it. If you've cut back on drinking, this is the phase where you can decide whether to add it back — with the rule still in place.

steps.title: Have a plan for the three big nights
steps.details: Once a week, look at the week ahead and name the one or two nights or events where a cigarette is most likely — a night out, a stressful day, a meal with people who smoke — and decide now what you'll do.

how_to.gist: Name the week's riskiest night and decide your move in advance.
how_to.why: The routine handles ordinary days. The nights out are where a quit quietly ends, and they're the ones you can see coming.

sections.heading: The look-ahead
items: Which night is riskiest this week
What you'll say if offered one

sections.heading: The exit line
sections.body: "I've packed it in." Short, boring, and it ends the conversation. You don't have to explain yourself to anyone.

sections.heading: If you're going to smoke
sections.body: Better to skip the event than to go and lose the quit. There'll be other nights out; there's only one of these quits.

how_to.counts_as_done: You picked out this week's riskiest night and decided what you'll do.

steps.title: Check in with your person
steps.details: Weekly update continues — how the week went, and anything that's starting to feel shaky.

phases.title: Off the patches, quit for good
phases.focus: Finish the patch course, hold zero cigarettes with nothing on board, and lock in the routines as the way you live now rather than a plan you're following.

steps.title: No cigarettes at all
steps.details: Zero, with nothing on board. This is the last stretch — the same rule, and by now the easiest one to keep.
steps.week_progression: Zero every day, now with no patches — the quit standing on its own.

steps.title: Finish the patch course
steps.details: Wear the patch until the course the pharmacist set out is complete, then stop. Don't stop early because you feel fine — and don't keep going past the end out of nerves.

how_to.gist: Wear the patch to the end of the course, then stop for good.
how_to.why: The whole point of the taper, the date, and the step-down was to get you to this: no cigarettes and no nicotine, without a cliff edge.

sections.heading: The finish
sections.body: Follow the course to its last day, then take the patch off and don't replace it. The physical withdrawal finished weeks ago.

sections.heading: The first patch-free days
sections.body: You may notice the habit of putting one on more than the nicotine. That's a routine, and routines fade in a week or so.

sections.heading: If it wobbles
sections.body: A rough patch-free week is a reason to talk to your person or the pharmacist, not a reason to buy a pack.

how_to.counts_as_done: You're on the patch if the course calls for it, or finished if it doesn't.

steps.title: Keep the after-meal ten minutes
steps.details: Still ten minutes up and moving after every meal. This one stays — it's the routine that replaced the cigarette, and it's yours now.

steps.title: Keep the drink hour script
steps.details: Evening drink, second drink, snack, no cigarette. Same rule as always — if you want to smoke, you leave the drink.

steps.title: Plan for the nights that could still catch you
steps.details: Keep the weekly look-ahead going — name the riskiest night, decide your move, and know your exit line.

steps.title: Weekly check-in with your person
steps.details: One honest update a week, same as before. By now it's mostly good news — say that too.

milestones.title: Down to 3 a day
milestones.criteria: Two weeks of counting, and the last week held at 3 cigarettes a day or fewer. Quit date is written down and the patches are in the house.

milestones.title: A month with no cigarettes
milestones.criteria: Thirty days from quit day with zero cigarettes, a patch on every morning, and the after-meal and drink-hour routines still running.

milestones.title: Three months clean, patches stepping down
milestones.criteria: Twelve weeks with no cigarettes and the patch strength stepped down on the schedule the pharmacist set.

milestones.title: Four months, no cigarettes, nothing on board
milestones.criteria: Sixteen weeks from the start, zero cigarettes, the patch course finished, and the after-meal and drink-hour routines still in place.

protocol.coach_notes: You've quit for two weeks twice — that's not a failure record, that's proof you can do the hard part. What you never had was a runway and something on board, and now you have both. Week two is coming; you know its name, you've told someone about it, and you've got a script for the drink hour it walks through. One missed day is noise. The day after a miss is the one that decides this — that's the rep that matters, and you've already shown you can take it.

protocol.goal_statement: Walk 10,000 steps a day, most days, built from a lunchtime park loop plus an after-work walk.
protocol.short_title: Walk 10,000 steps a day in 10 weeks

phases.title: The two slots
phases.focus: Get the lunch loop and the after-work walk happening on workdays, at a size that feels almost too easy.

steps.title: Lunchtime park loop
steps.details: Leave the desk at lunch and walk the park by the office for 15 minutes. Same route each day so you stop deciding and just go. Shoes and a jacket live under the desk so nothing has to be fetched first.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 15 minutes. It should feel like you could easily do more — that's the point.

how_to.gist: Walk the park by the office for 15 minutes at lunch.
how_to.why: This is the single biggest piece of your 10,000 steps. Twenty-five minutes in that park is roughly half the gap between where you are and where you're going, and it's already sitting outside your office door.

sections.heading: The setup
sections.body: Tonight, put a pair of walking shoes and a light jacket under your desk. Tomorrow at lunch you should be able to stand up and go without going anywhere else first.

sections.heading: The loop
sections.body: Walk out of the building, into the park, and follow the same path every day. Pick it once and stop thinking about it. Fifteen minutes out and back, or a loop that lands you back at the door.

sections.heading: If lunch gets eaten
sections.body: Some days a meeting will take the slot. That's fine — the after-work walk is still there, and a short one still counts. What you don't do is let one lost lunch turn into a lost week.

how_to.counts_as_done: You left the building and walked the park for at least 15 minutes.

steps.title: After-work walk
steps.details: On workdays, walk 15 minutes after you finish. Go straight from the car, or park a few streets further from home and walk the rest. This is the walk that turns a good day into a 10,000-step day.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 15 minutes. Weeks 4-7: 20 minutes. Weeks 8-10: 25 minutes.

how_to.gist: Walk 15 minutes after work before you go inside.
how_to.why: The lunch loop gets you halfway. This is the other half — without it you land around 7,000 and the goal stays out of reach.

sections.heading: The trick
sections.body: Don't go home first. Once you're through your own front door the day is over. Park a few streets away, or step out of the car and start walking before you've decided anything.

sections.heading: Where
sections.body: Anywhere. Around the block, down to the shops, a loop of the neighbourhood. It doesn't need to be the park or anything scenic — it needs to be 15 minutes of moving.

sections.heading: The floor day
sections.body: On days when the lunch loop didn't happen, this walk is what saves the day. Do it anyway, even if it's short. Ten minutes still beats zero, and it keeps the run going.

how_to.counts_as_done: You walked at least 15 minutes after finishing work.

steps.title: Hit your daily step floor
steps.details: Every day, including weekends, land at 6,000 steps or more. That's your current average plus a bit — small enough that a normal day gets there, big enough that it isn't nothing.

how_to.gist: Finish the day at 6,000 steps or more.
how_to.why: You're at about 4,000 now. Asking for 10,000 on day one is how walking plans die in week two — this is the same goal with the ramp left in.

sections.heading: The number
sections.body: 6,000 steps, every day, weekends included. Check it whenever you like — once at lunch, once in the evening is plenty.

sections.heading: How it moves
sections.body: It goes up about 1,500 steps every three or four weeks, not every week. By the last stretch you'll be at 9,000 as a floor, and 10,000 will be an ordinary day rather than a push.

sections.heading: Weekends
sections.body: Weekends count. A Saturday with no walk in it is where a 4,000-step baseline comes back from. A single longer walk usually covers it.

how_to.counts_as_done: The app shows 6,000 or more steps for the day.

steps.title: Shoes and jacket by the desk
steps.details: One-time setup, done before week one starts: walking shoes and a light jacket under your desk at work, and a second pair by the front door at home. Nothing to fetch, nothing to remember.

how_to.gist: Put walking shoes under your desk and by your front door.
how_to.why: Every extra step between you and the walk is a chance to not go. Removing them is the cheapest thing you'll do all plan.

sections.heading: Do this once
items: Walking shoes and a jacket under your desk at work
A second pair of shoes by the front door at home
Check the park entrance on your way in tomorrow so you know exactly where you're going

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: If the shoes are in the car boot or in a cupboard, the walk becomes a decision. If they're under the desk, it becomes a thing you just do.

how_to.counts_as_done: Shoes are under your desk at work and by the door at home.

steps.title: One longer weekend walk
steps.details: Once each weekend, take a 30-minute walk somewhere you actually like going. This is the day that makes up ground and the one that reminds you walking is pleasant rather than a chore.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 30 minutes. Weeks 4-7: 45 minutes. Weeks 8-10: 60 minutes.

how_to.gist: Take one 30-minute walk on the weekend, somewhere you like.
how_to.why: Weekdays are structured and busy. A weekend walk is where you get ahead on steps and where walking stops feeling like a task.

sections.heading: Pick the day
sections.body: Saturday or Sunday, whichever is quieter. Put it in the morning if you can — it's done before the day gets away from you.

sections.heading: Pick the place
sections.body: Somewhere you'd go anyway or somewhere you've been meaning to. A park, a canal, a bit of town. It doesn't need to be exercise, it needs to be a walk.

sections.heading: Optional company
sections.body: If someone will come with you, bring them. A walk with a person is a walk you'll repeat.

how_to.counts_as_done: One walk of 30 minutes or more happened on the weekend.

phases.title: Longer, not harder
phases.focus: The same two slots, stretched. The lunch loop becomes a proper 25-minute walk and the daily floor climbs.

steps.title: Lunchtime park loop
steps.details: The same park loop, now 25 minutes. Same route, same shoes under the desk. If 25 minutes doesn't fit the lunch break, do 20 and add the rest to the evening walk.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-7: 25 minutes.

how_to.gist: Stretch the lunch park loop to 25 minutes.
how_to.why: You've done three weeks at 15. Twenty-five minutes in the park is now roughly 3,000 steps on its own — half the daily target from one lunch break.

sections.heading: The stretch
sections.body: Add ten minutes to the same loop. Walk a bit further into the park, or go round twice. Keep the route identical so the only thing that changed is the length.

sections.heading: If lunch is short
sections.body: Some days you'll only have 20 minutes. Take the 20 and make it up in the evening rather than skipping the walk entirely.

how_to.counts_as_done: You walked the park for at least 25 minutes at lunch.

steps.title: After-work walk
steps.details: Twenty minutes after work, before you go inside. Same rule as before: don't sit down first.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-7: 20 minutes.

how_to.gist: Walk 20 minutes after work before going inside.
how_to.why: This is the walk that decides whether the day lands at 7,000 or at 10,000. It's also the one that saves a day when lunch got taken by a meeting.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Straight out of the car, or park further away and walk the last stretch home. Twenty minutes, then you're done and the evening is yours.

sections.heading: When it's the only walk
sections.body: On days the lunch loop didn't happen, this is your floor day. Do it anyway. A short walk on a bad day is worth more than a perfect walk you didn't take.

how_to.counts_as_done: You walked at least 20 minutes after finishing work.

steps.title: Hit your daily step floor
steps.details: 7,500 steps every day, weekends included. The two walks on a workday should get you most of the way there without any extra effort.

how_to.gist: Finish the day at 7,500 steps or more.
how_to.why: You've been holding 6,000 for three weeks. This is the next small step up — about 1,500 more than last month, not a new life.

sections.heading: The number
sections.body: 7,500 a day, every day. On workdays the two walks plus your normal moving around should cover it. On weekends the longer walk does the work.

sections.heading: If you're short at 9pm
sections.body: A ten-minute walk around the block closes most of a gap. Do that rather than writing the day off.

how_to.counts_as_done: The app shows 7,500 or more steps for the day.

steps.title: One longer weekend walk
steps.details: Forty-five minutes once each weekend, somewhere you enjoy. This is the day that keeps the weekly average up and keeps walking feeling like something you choose.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-7: 45 minutes. Weeks 8-10: 60 minutes.

how_to.gist: Take one 45-minute walk on the weekend.
how_to.why: Weekend walks are where the ground gets made up. They're also the reason this stays a habit rather than a chore — you're going somewhere you like.

sections.heading: The stretch
sections.body: Same as the 30-minute version, just longer. Go further along the same route, or pick somewhere new that needs the extra time.

sections.heading: Keep it pleasant
sections.body: If 45 minutes starts to feel like a punishment, drop back to 30 and add the time to a weekday instead. The walk you enjoy is the walk you keep doing.

how_to.counts_as_done: One walk of 45 minutes or more happened on the weekend.

steps.title: Take the stairs and the long way
steps.details: On workdays, take the stairs instead of the lift and walk the long way to the kitchen, the printer, the meeting room. Small, free steps that pad out a desk day.

how_to.gist: Stairs instead of the lift, long way round at work.
how_to.why: A desk job means the day has almost no movement in it unless you put some there. These are the steps that cost you nothing and add up quietly.

sections.heading: The small rules
items: Stairs, not the lift, every time
Long way to the kitchen and the printer
Stand up and walk for two minutes once an hour
Walk to a colleague's desk instead of messaging them

sections.heading: Why bother
sections.body: None of these is a workout. Together they're often 1,000-1,500 steps a day you were going to spend sitting down anyway.

how_to.counts_as_done: You took the stairs and the long way round at work today.

phases.title: 10,000 as an ordinary day
phases.focus: The floor reaches 9,000 and the two walks carry you past 10,000 on most days without anything extra.

steps.title: Lunchtime park loop
steps.details: Thirty minutes in the park at lunch. This is your full lunch break walk — roughly 3,500 steps on its own.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 8-10: 30 minutes.

how_to.gist: Walk the park for the full 30 minutes at lunch.
how_to.why: Thirty minutes in the park is now more than a third of your daily target from one break in the middle of the day.

sections.heading: The full loop
sections.body: Same route, thirty minutes. If you've been doing 25, this is one more stretch of the same path.

sections.heading: Protect the slot
sections.body: By now this is the fixed point of your workday. Treat it like a meeting you don't move — it's the thing everything else hangs off.

how_to.counts_as_done: You walked the park for at least 30 minutes at lunch.

steps.title: After-work walk
steps.details: Twenty-five minutes after work. With the lunch loop, this is what puts a normal workday over 10,000.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 8-10: 25 minutes.

how_to.gist: Walk 25 minutes after work before going inside.
how_to.why: Lunch loop plus this walk is the whole plan working. On a workday, these two together are 10,000 steps.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Out of the car and walking, or park further away and cover the last stretch on foot. Twenty-five minutes, then in.

sections.heading: The floor day
sections.body: If lunch was lost, this is still here. Do it, even shortened. The day you walk after a bad day is the day the habit survives.

how_to.counts_as_done: You walked at least 25 minutes after finishing work.

steps.title: Hit your daily step floor
steps.details: 9,000 steps every day, weekends included. On workdays the two walks get you there. Weekends need the longer walk.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 8-10: 9,000. Ten thousand becomes the ordinary workday, not the target.

how_to.gist: Finish the day at 9,000 steps or more.
how_to.why: This is the last step of the ramp. Hold 9,000 as a floor and 10,000 stops being something you chase and starts being a normal Tuesday.

sections.heading: The number
sections.body: 9,000 a day, every day. Most workdays you'll clear 10,000 without trying — the floor is there for the days that go sideways.

sections.heading: The last stretch
sections.body: If you're at 8,000 at nine in the evening, a fifteen-minute walk closes it. That's the whole remaining job.

how_to.counts_as_done: The app shows 9,000 or more steps for the day.

steps.title: One longer weekend walk
steps.details: An hour once each weekend. This is the walk that makes the weekly average comfortable and the one you'll keep doing after the ten weeks are up.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 8-10: 60 minutes.

how_to.gist: Take one 60-minute walk on the weekend.
how_to.why: An hour on the weekend is roughly 6,000 steps in one go. It's also the most enjoyable walk of your week, which is why it's the one that lasts.

sections.heading: The hour
sections.body: Same place or somewhere new. An hour is long enough to get somewhere worth getting to — a park, a river, a bit of town you don't usually see.

sections.heading: Bring someone
sections.body: If there's a person who'd come, ask them. An hour goes quickly with company and it's much harder to skip.

how_to.counts_as_done: One walk of 60 minutes or more happened on the weekend.

steps.title: Plan the next month of walks
steps.details: Once, in the last two weeks, sit down for ten minutes and decide how the walking continues after this plan ends. Which walks stay, which days, and what your new normal floor is.

how_to.gist: Spend ten minutes deciding how the walking continues after week 10.
how_to.why: Ten weeks gets you to 10,000 steps. What keeps you there is deciding, before the plan ends, which parts of it you're keeping.

sections.heading: What to decide
items: Which walks stay — both, or just the lunch loop
What your everyday floor is now (9,000 is a good answer)
What you'll do on the days it doesn't happen

sections.heading: Write it down
sections.body: Two or three lines somewhere you'll see them. A plan you've said out loud is much harder to quietly abandon.

how_to.counts_as_done: You've written down which walks you're keeping and on which days.

milestones.title: Three weeks of two walks a day
milestones.criteria: The lunch loop and the after-work walk both happened on most workdays for three straight weeks, and the daily floor never dropped below 6,000.

milestones.title: The floor is 7,500
milestones.criteria: Seven weeks in, 7,500 steps is a normal day rather than a target, and the lunch loop has grown from 15 minutes to 25.

milestones.title: 10,000 is an ordinary workday
milestones.criteria: Most days land at or above 10,000 steps, the daily floor sits at 9,000, and you've written down which walks you're keeping after the plan ends.

protocol.coach_notes: You already did the hard part — you know exactly where these steps come from. A park by the office and a walk after work are two real slots in a real day, and that's more than most people start with. The only thing that will decide this is what happens on the days one of them doesn't. One missed lunch is noise. The walk you take the day after a missed lunch is the one that builds the habit — so never miss twice. Ten weeks from now, 10,000 steps won't be a goal you're chasing; it'll just be what a Tuesday looks like.
