protocol.goal_statement: Walk 10,000 steps a day consistently, built from a 4,000-step baseline via a lunch walk and an after-work walk.
protocol.short_title: Walk 10,000 steps a day in 10 weeks

phases.title: Two walks, every workday
phases.focus: Get the lunch walk and the after-work walk to happen on all five workdays, at a length that feels almost too easy. The number takes care of itself once the two windows are real.

steps.title: Lunch walk
steps.details: Out the door within 10 minutes of finishing lunch, 20 minutes of steady walking, same route each day. Shoes live under your desk so nothing stands between you and the door.

how_to.gist: 20 minutes out the door within 10 minutes of finishing lunch, same route daily.
how_to.why: This is the window you named yourself, and it's the one a busy day eats first. Making it the same route at the same time means you don't have to decide anything — you just go.

sections.heading: The setup
sections.body: Keep your walking shoes under your desk, not in a bag or at home. The night before, know what you're doing for lunch so the walk isn't competing with a food run.

sections.heading: The walk
items: Back at your desk before your next thing

sections.heading: If the day fights back
sections.body: A 10-minute version still counts as showing up — but only use it when the day genuinely leaves you no room, not when you'd rather not. If lunch gets eaten by a meeting, the walk moves to the first free 20 minutes after it, same day.

how_to.counts_as_done: 20 minutes of walking between finishing lunch and your next commitment — 5 days this week.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 20 minutes each workday. Length stays put while the habit settles.

steps.title: After-work walk
steps.details: 20 minutes on your feet after work, before you sit down for the evening. Change out of work clothes first, then straight out — the couch is what beats this one.

how_to.gist: 20 minutes walking after work, before you sit down for the evening.
how_to.why: The second window you named. The trick is order: walk before you sit, because once you're on the couch this one is gone.

sections.heading: Where
sections.body: Anywhere — around the block, to the shop and back, a loop you like. It doesn't need to be a workout. It needs to be 20 minutes of not sitting.

sections.heading: Late days
sections.body: If work runs long, the walk still happens when you get in — even if it's dark, even if it's shorter. A 10-minute loop after a late finish keeps the day alive; skipping it entirely is what starts the slide.

how_to.counts_as_done: 20 minutes of walking after work, before you sat down for the evening — 5 days this week.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 20 minutes each workday, right after getting home.

steps.title: Saturday long walk
steps.details: One longer walk on Saturday — 40 minutes somewhere you actually like walking. This is the day that pads the week's total and gives you room to miss a weekday without the week falling apart.

how_to.gist: One 40-minute walk on Saturday, somewhere you enjoy walking.
how_to.why: Weekdays are where the habit lives; Saturday is where the cushion comes from. One longer walk means a rained-out Tuesday doesn't wreck the week.

sections.heading: Pick the place
sections.body: A park, a waterfront, a neighbourhood you like — somewhere you'd walk anyway. If it's a place you enjoy, this day stops being a chore and starts being the good part of the week.

sections.heading: The walk
sections.body: 40 minutes, steady, no pace target. Bring something to listen to if that helps you keep going.

sections.heading: If Saturday goes
sections.body: Move it to Sunday rather than dropping it. The long walk is the week's shock absorber — it's the one you protect hardest.

how_to.counts_as_done: 40 minutes of walking on Saturday or Sunday.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 40 minutes. Grows to 60 in phase 2.

steps.title: Daily step target
steps.details: 6,000 steps a day, from your normal day plus the two walks. Check your phone or watch at the end of the day — if you're short, a 10-minute loop closes the gap.

how_to.gist: Hit 6,000 steps a day — your normal 4,000 plus the two walks.
how_to.why: You already do about 4,000 without trying. The two walks add roughly 2,000 more, so 6,000 is what your day looks like when the walks happen. It's a check, not a stretch.

sections.heading: The number
sections.body: 6,000 steps. Your baseline day is around 4,000; the lunch and after-work walks carry the rest. If you hit the walks, this number hits itself.

sections.heading: When to check
sections.body: Once, in the evening. If you're close, a 10-minute loop around the block finishes it. If you're miles off, look at which walk didn't happen rather than trying to walk it back at 10pm.

sections.heading: The floor
sections.body: On a day that goes sideways, 4,000 is the floor — your normal day. Never below that. A day at your old baseline is a neutral day, not a lost one.

how_to.counts_as_done: The app shows 6,000+ steps for the day.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 6,000/day. Rises to 7,500 in phase 2 and 9,000 in phase 3.

steps.title: Weekly step floor
steps.details: 42,000 steps across the week — an average of 6,000 a day, but graded on the total. A bad Tuesday gets absorbed by a good Saturday instead of breaking anything.

how_to.gist: 42,000 steps across the whole week — the total is what counts, not any single day.
how_to.why: Grading the week instead of the day is what keeps one bad day from becoming a bad week. Life will eat a day here and there; the week total is what you're actually building.

sections.heading: The maths
sections.body: 6,000 a day times seven is 42,000. You don't need 6,000 every single day — you need 42,000 by Sunday night.

sections.heading: How to use it
sections.body: Check it Saturday. If you're behind, the Saturday long walk is where you catch up. If you're ahead, you've bought yourself slack for a rough day next week.

sections.heading: What it protects
sections.body: A missed lunch walk on a meeting-heavy Tuesday costs you nothing if Saturday is long. That's the point.

how_to.counts_as_done: The week's step total reads 42,000 or more by Sunday night.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 42,000/week. Rises with the daily target each phase.

phases.title: Longer walks, bigger days
phases.focus: The two walks are happening. Now they get longer and the daily number climbs — same windows, more time in them.

steps.title: Lunch walk
steps.details: Lunch walk grows to 30 minutes. Same route, same trigger, ten more minutes on it.

how_to.gist: 30 minutes out the door within 10 minutes of finishing lunch.
how_to.why: The habit is holding, so the walk earns more time. Ten extra minutes here is the cheapest step increase you have — you're already out the door.

sections.heading: The change
sections.body: Same route, same timing, 30 minutes instead of 20. If 30 feels like a lot in week 4, hold at 25 for a few days and build to 30 by week 5.

sections.heading: Keep the trigger
sections.body: Shoes under the desk, out within 10 minutes of finishing lunch. The length changed; nothing else did.

how_to.counts_as_done: 30 minutes of walking in the lunch window — 5 days this week.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-7: 30 minutes each workday.

steps.title: After-work walk
steps.details: After-work walk grows to 30 minutes. Still before you sit down — that order is what makes it happen.

how_to.gist: 30 minutes walking after work, still before you sit down.
how_to.why: Same window, more time. The before-you-sit rule is doing the heavy lifting here — don't trade it for a longer walk.

sections.heading: The change
sections.body: 30 minutes instead of 20. Same loop, or extend it by a street or two.

how_to.counts_as_done: 30 minutes of walking after work, before sitting down — 5 days this week.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-7: 30 minutes each workday.

steps.title: Saturday long walk
steps.details: Saturday walk grows to 60 minutes. This is now a proper outing — pick somewhere worth an hour.

how_to.gist: One 60-minute walk on Saturday, somewhere worth an hour.
how_to.why: An hour on Saturday is what makes the daily number reachable without cramming walks into every spare minute of the workweek.

sections.heading: The walk
sections.body: 60 minutes, steady. Bring water if it's warm, and something to listen to if you like.

sections.heading: If it's too much
sections.body: Split it — 30 minutes in the morning, 30 in the afternoon. Two shorter walks on Saturday count the same as one long one.

how_to.counts_as_done: 60 minutes of walking on Saturday or Sunday.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-7: 60 minutes.

steps.title: Daily step target
steps.details: 7,500 steps a day. The longer walks carry most of the increase — the rest comes from taking the stairs and walking to the far printer instead of the near one.

how_to.gist: Hit 7,500 steps a day — the longer walks do most of the work.
how_to.why: You're three weeks in with the walks holding. This is the next honest step up, and it's mostly paid for by the ten extra minutes on each walk.

sections.heading: The number
sections.body: 7,500 steps. Two 30-minute walks plus your normal day gets you most of the way there. The last few hundred come from small choices — stairs, the far printer, walking to someone instead of messaging them.

sections.heading: The floor
sections.body: 5,000 is the floor on a bad day. Below your old baseline is the only real failure.

sections.heading: If you're consistently short
sections.body: Add 10 minutes to whichever walk is easier that day rather than trying to find a third walk. Two windows, more time in them.

how_to.counts_as_done: The app shows 7,500+ steps for the day.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-7: 7,500/day.

steps.title: Weekly step floor
steps.details: 52,500 steps across the week — 7,500 a day on average, graded on the total.

how_to.gist: 52,500 steps across the week — the total, not any single day.
how_to.why: Same rule as before, bigger number. The week total is what absorbs a bad day without it turning into a bad week.

sections.heading: The maths
sections.body: 7,500 a day times seven is 52,500. Check it Saturday and use the long walk to close any gap.

sections.heading: The point
sections.body: You're allowed a 4,000-step day. You're not allowed a 4,000-step week.

how_to.counts_as_done: The week's step total reads 52,500 or more by Sunday night.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-7: 52,500/week.

phases.title: Ten thousand, held
phases.focus: The daily number reaches 10,000 and stays there. The walks are the engine; the small choices fill the last stretch.

steps.title: Lunch walk
steps.details: Lunch walk at 35 minutes. This is close to its final length — the walk is now a fixture of the workday, not an add-on.

how_to.gist: 35 minutes out the door within 10 minutes of finishing lunch.
how_to.why: This is the last increase on the lunch walk. From here it just needs to keep happening.

sections.heading: The change
sections.body: 35 minutes. Same route, extended slightly, or the same loop walked a touch faster.

sections.heading: Holding it
sections.body: At this length the walk is a real part of your day. The only thing that threatens it is a week where you let the trigger slip — shoes back in the bag, out the door late. Keep the shoes under the desk.

how_to.counts_as_done: 35 minutes of walking in the lunch window — 5 days this week.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 8-10: 35 minutes each workday.

steps.title: After-work walk
steps.details: After-work walk at 35 minutes, still before you sit down.

how_to.gist: 35 minutes walking after work, still before you sit down.
how_to.why: The evening walk is what gets you over the line on days when the lunch window got eaten. It's the reliable one.

sections.heading: The change
sections.body: 35 minutes instead of 30. Same order: home, change, shoes, walk, then sit.

sections.heading: Dark evenings
sections.body: If it's dark by the time you get out, stick to lit streets and keep the loop short and familiar. The walk still counts.

how_to.counts_as_done: 35 minutes of walking after work, before sitting down — 5 days this week.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 8-10: 35 minutes each workday.

steps.title: Saturday long walk
steps.details: Saturday walk holds at 60 minutes. It's the cushion that makes the 10,000 a day survivable across a whole week.

how_to.gist: One 60-minute walk on Saturday — the week's cushion.
how_to.why: With the daily target at 10,000, the long walk is what lets you have a lighter day midweek without the week total suffering.

sections.heading: The walk
sections.body: 60 minutes, somewhere you like. No pace target.

sections.heading: Why it stays
sections.body: Don't drop this one now that the daily number is high. It's the reason a rough Wednesday doesn't cost you the week.

how_to.counts_as_done: 60 minutes of walking on Saturday or Sunday.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 8-10: 60 minutes.

steps.title: Daily step target
steps.details: 10,000 steps a day. Two 35-minute walks plus your normal day gets you close; the last stretch comes from taking the stairs, walking to lunch, and standing up every hour.

how_to.gist: Hit 10,000 steps a day — the number you set out for.
how_to.why: This is the goal. It's reachable now because the two walks are already happening and the ramp got you here without a single heroic day.

sections.heading: The floor
sections.body: 6,000 is the floor on a genuinely bad day. One low day is noise; two in a row is the thing to catch.

sections.heading: If you're short at 9pm
sections.body: A 15-minute loop around the block closes most of a gap. Do that rather than writing the day off.

how_to.counts_as_done: The app shows 10,000+ steps for the day.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 8-10: 10,000/day, held steady. No further increases — this is the destination.

steps.title: Weekly step floor
steps.details: 70,000 steps across the week — 10,000 a day on average. This is the number that says the habit is real, not the streak.

how_to.gist: 70,000 steps across the week — the whole week at your target.
how_to.why: Hitting 10,000 seven days running is a nice story; hitting 70,000 in a week is the actual goal. The week total is what you're building.

sections.heading: The maths
sections.body: 10,000 a day times seven is 70,000. Check it Saturday, use the long walk to close a gap.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Never miss twice. A 6,000-step Monday costs you nothing if Tuesday is back at 10,000. Two low days in a row is the only pattern worth worrying about.

how_to.counts_as_done: The week's step total reads 70,000 or more by Sunday night.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 8-10: 70,000/week.

milestones.title: Two walks, five days a week
milestones.criteria: Three straight weeks where the lunch walk and the after-work walk both happened on all five workdays, and the week's steps cleared 42,000 each time.

milestones.title: The walks got longer without a fight
milestones.criteria: Two weeks at 30 minutes per walk, five workdays a week, with the week total clearing 52,500.

milestones.title: A 7,500-step day feels normal
milestones.criteria: The daily number has been 7,500 or more for most of the week, and a low day no longer feels like a failure — it feels like a low day.

milestones.title: Ten thousand a day, held for three weeks
milestones.criteria: Three consecutive weeks averaging 10,000 steps a day, with the lunch and after-work walks still happening on workdays.

protocol.coach_notes: You're not building movement from nothing — you already walk 4,000 steps a day without thinking about it. This plan just adds two windows you picked yourself and gives them more time each phase. The number climbs on its own from there. The one thing that decides this is what happens after a missed day: one low day is noise, the walk you take the day after is the one that matters. Never miss twice.

protocol.goal_statement: Run a continuous 4k — starting from zero running, three mornings a week, built over ten weeks instead of six.

phases.title: Get out the door
phases.focus: Three mornings a week, mostly walking with short running bouts. The job this phase is showing up and getting your legs used to running at all.

steps.title: Monday morning walk/run
steps.details: Out the door before work for about 25 minutes: walk 3 minutes, then run 1 minute, and keep alternating that 3-and-1 all the way round. The running minutes are meant to feel almost too short — that's the point.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: hold the same 3 minutes walking / 1 minute running pattern. The win is the three mornings, not the speed.

how_to.gist: 25 minutes: alternate 3 minutes brisk walking with 1 minute of easy running.
how_to.why: You've never run before, so week one is about your legs meeting the ground gently, three times, without anything hurting. Short running bouts build the base without the shin and knee flare that kills beginner plans.

sections.heading: The pattern
items: Run 1 minute, slow enough to talk
Repeat until you're back at your start
Finish with 3-4 minutes of walking to cool down

sections.heading: The pace
sections.body: The running minute should feel easier than you expect — if you're gasping at the end of it, slow down. You should be able to say a short sentence out loud while running. Walking briskly is not cheating; it's the other half of the session.

sections.heading: If it hurts
sections.body: Muscle tiredness is fine. Sharp pain, or anything in your shins or knees that gets worse as you go, means stop and walk home. Take two rest days, then repeat the same session rather than moving forward.

how_to.counts_as_done: 25 minutes out the door, walk/run pattern followed, back home.

steps.title: Wednesday morning walk/run
steps.details: Same 25 minutes as Monday — 3 minutes walking, 1 minute running, alternating. A day of rest between sessions is what lets your legs absorb Monday.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: unchanged pattern. Same distance, same effort, three mornings.

how_to.gist: Same as Monday: 3 minutes walking, 1 minute running, 25 minutes total.
how_to.why: The second session of the week is where the habit starts to feel normal rather than novel. Keeping it identical to Monday means there's nothing new to think about at 6am.

sections.heading: The pattern
items: Walk the last few minutes home

sections.heading: Keep it the same
sections.body: Don't add running minutes on a good day. The plan adds them for you, on a schedule your legs can keep up with. A session that feels easy is a session that's working.

how_to.counts_as_done: 25 minutes out the door, walk/run pattern followed, back home.

steps.title: Friday morning walk/run
steps.details: Third session of the week, same 3-and-1 pattern, 25 minutes. Three mornings done is the whole goal of this phase.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: unchanged. Three sessions a week, never back-to-back days.

how_to.gist: Third session: 3 minutes walking, 1 minute running, 25 minutes total.
how_to.why: Three mornings a week is the dose this build needs, and Friday closes the week. Getting all three in is what makes next week's slightly longer running bouts possible.

sections.heading: After this one
sections.body: Two days off before Monday. That gap isn't slack — it's when your legs actually get stronger. Don't add a fourth session, however good you feel.

how_to.counts_as_done: 25 minutes out the door, walk/run pattern followed, back home.

steps.title: Kit by the door the night before
steps.details: The night before each running morning, put your trainers, socks and whatever you wear out by the front door, and set your alarm before you sit down for the evening. Nothing to find, nothing to decide at 6am.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: every night before a running morning. By phase two this should be automatic — if it isn't, keep it.

how_to.gist: Night before each run: trainers and clothes by the door, alarm set.
how_to.why: The gap between deciding to run and actually being outside is where beginner plans die. Removing every small decision from the morning makes the only remaining step walking out of the door.

sections.heading: What to set out
items: Trainers and socks, side by side
Water bottle if you take one
Alarm set before you sit down for the evening

sections.heading: Why the night before
sections.body: At 6am you're not making decisions, you're following a path you already laid. Clothes by the door means the first thing you do is put them on.

how_to.counts_as_done: Kit out and alarm set the night before each of the three running mornings.

steps.title: One full rest day between runs
steps.details: The days after each running morning are walking-only. A brisk walk is fine and good; running on back-to-back days is not, at this stage. Your legs adapt on the days off, not on the days on.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: strictly no running on rest days. Later phases keep the same spacing.

how_to.gist: No running on the days between sessions — walking is fine.
how_to.why: New runners get hurt by running on consecutive days long before they get hurt by running too far. The rest day is part of the training, not a break from it.

sections.heading: What counts
items: A long walk in the park: yes
A run, even a short one: no
Two rest days after Friday's session

sections.heading: If you're itching to go
sections.body: Feeling good is the reason to hold back, not to add a session. The plan adds running minutes for you every week — trust the schedule rather than your mood.

how_to.counts_as_done: No running on the three days between sessions.

phases.title: Running gets longer
phases.focus: The running bouts grow and the walking shrinks. Same three mornings, same park, more time actually running.

steps.title: Monday morning intervals
steps.details: 30 minutes now. Weeks 4-5: walk 2 minutes, run 2 minutes. Weeks 6-7: walk 1 minute, run 3 minutes. The running stretches out while the walking shrinks.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-5: 2 min walk / 2 min run. Weeks 6-7: 1 min walk / 3 min run.

how_to.gist: 30 minutes alternating walking and running, with the running getting longer each fortnight.
how_to.why: This is where the running actually starts to accumulate. Doubling the running bout from one minute to two, then three, is the same gentle step you took in week one — just repeated.

sections.heading: The pattern
items: Weeks 4-5: walk 2 minutes, run 2 minutes, repeat
Weeks 6-7: walk 1 minute, run 3 minutes, repeat
Walk the last few minutes to cool down

sections.heading: The pace
sections.body: Still conversational. If you can't speak a short sentence while running, you're going too fast — slow down rather than shortening the running bout. Slower is how you get further.

sections.heading: If it hurts
sections.body: Sharp or worsening pain in shins, knees or feet: stop, take two rest days, and repeat the previous week's pattern rather than moving on.

how_to.counts_as_done: 30 minutes out the door, this fortnight's walk/run pattern followed.

steps.title: Wednesday morning intervals
steps.details: Same 30 minutes and same pattern as Monday. Keeping the two sessions identical means one thing to remember, not two.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-5: 2 min walk / 2 min run. Weeks 6-7: 1 min walk / 3 min run.

how_to.gist: Same as Monday: 30 minutes, this fortnight's walk/run pattern.
how_to.why: The middle session of the week is the one most likely to get skipped once the novelty wears off. Making it a carbon copy of Monday removes the excuse that you can't remember what you're meant to be doing.

sections.heading: If you're short on time
sections.body: Do the pattern for 20 minutes rather than skipping it. A shortened session keeps the week intact; a skipped one breaks the chain.

how_to.counts_as_done: 30 minutes out the door, this fortnight's walk/run pattern followed.

steps.title: Friday morning intervals
steps.details: Third session, same 30 minutes and pattern. Three mornings done again this week.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-5: 2 min walk / 2 min run. Weeks 6-7: 1 min walk / 3 min run.

how_to.gist: Third session: 30 minutes, this fortnight's walk/run pattern.
how_to.why: Three sessions a week is what makes the jump to continuous running possible at the end. Friday is the one that completes the week.

sections.heading: After this one
sections.body: Two rest days, then Monday. Don't add a fourth session even if the running is starting to feel good — the spacing is doing real work.

steps.details: Still no running on the days between sessions. Walking is welcome. This matters more now, not less — the running bouts are longer and your legs need the gap.

phases.focus: The walking shrinks to almost nothing, then disappears. Same three mornings, one continuous run at the end of it.

steps.title: Monday morning run
steps.details: Week 8: run 5 minutes, walk 1 minute, repeat. Week 9: run 8 minutes, walk 1 minute, repeat. Week 10: run the whole 4k without stopping.

how_to.gist: The walking breaks shrink to one minute, then vanish — continuous 4k by week 10.
how_to.why: This is the phase the whole ten weeks was built for. Each step up is small enough that your legs barely notice, which is how you arrive at a continuous 4k without a single jump you weren't ready for.

sections.heading: The pace
sections.body: Slower than you think. The goal is continuous, not fast — a pace you could hold a broken conversation at is the right one. If you need to walk in week 10, walk, then finish the distance running.

sections.heading: If it hurts
sections.body: Sharp or worsening pain: stop, two rest days, repeat the previous week rather than pushing on. A repeated week costs you seven days; an injury costs you the goal.

how_to.why: The middle session keeps the week from becoming a Monday-and-Friday-only habit. It's also the one that tells you whether the longer running bouts are landing comfortably.

sections.heading: Reading your legs
sections.body: If Wednesday feels harder than Monday, that's normal and not a reason to back off. If it hurts rather than tires, that is a reason to back off.

protocol.coach_notes: Ten weeks instead of six isn't a softer goal — it's the same finish line with a runway your legs can actually use. The three mornings are already the hard part, and you've got them fixed before work, which is more than most people manage. One missed morning is noise; the session after a miss is the one that decides this, so never let two go by. And if a shin or knee starts complaining, take the two rest days and repeat the week — that rule is the whole reason this plan is ten weeks long.
